item.title: Training Object Permanence in World Models
item.description: By Haotian Zhang, Fengyuan Yu, Dezhi Luo (University of Southern California, Carnegie Mellon University, Columbia University) Training Object Permanence in World Models. The first three authors are Haotian Zhang, Fengyuan Yu, and Dezhi Luo, from the University of Southern California, Carnegie Mellon University, and Columbia University, with a very long tail of coauthors across more than a dozen institutions, including Johns Hopkins, Oxford, Toronto, and Berkeley. The question this paper starts from is deceptively simple. A toddler knows, without any training data, that a ball hidden under a cup is still there when the cup lifts, and that a solid ball cannot pass through a solid wall. Those two priors, object permanence and solidity, are among the first things infants reliably demonstrate, and developmental psychologists have studied them for decades. Video generation models are increasingly treated as world models, systems that supposedly understand how the physical world works. But do they actually have object permanence in them, or do they just generate frames that look plausible while quietly violating the physics? No one had a clean way to ask, because no one had built a benchmark that isolates exactly those two cognitive abilities while holding everything else constant. That gap is what WROP fills. WROP, which stands for World Reasoning with Object Permanence, is a data infrastructure of one hundred and fifty hand-designed tasks, divided into six task families, each built around a generator written in Blender. The generators render the core cognitive scene, the occlusion, the barrier, the moving object, and then randomize everything that is not the cognition: lighting, camera angle, speed, background, and other nuisance parameters. item.title: OmniEcho: Audio-Visual Spatial Understanding for Omni-Modal Embodied Agents
item.description: By Ruixun Liu, Yuxuan Wang, Jiacheng Xie (Peking University, Alibaba Group, Tsinghua University) OmniEcho, Audio-Visual Spatial Understanding for Omni-Modal Embodied Agents. The first three authors are Ruixun Liu, Yuxuan Wang, and Jiacheng Xie, with the work coming out of Peking University's State Key Laboratory of General Artificial Intelligence, Alibaba's Token Hub, and Tsinghua University; part of the work was done during an internship at Alibaba. Humans do something with their ears that embodied agents still cannot: localize. You can close your eyes, hear a chair scrape, and turn your head in the right direction, then fuse that with what you see to reason about the room. The paper's starting point is that we do not actually know how to measure or model this in an agent setting. Most spatial audio research is done on synthetic, anechoic, or single-source data, and most embodied navigation research ignores audio entirely, treating the world as something you can only see. OmniEcho attacks both halves at once: a benchmark to measure spatial audio-visual understanding, and a model to learn it. The benchmark, OmniEchoBench, is built on real data, which is the hard part. It spans one hundred and ninety-seven real-world spatial audio-visual scenes, with two thousand nine hundred and seventy-two question-answer pairs and nine hundred navigation samples. The audio is recorded in first-order ambisonics, a four-channel format that captures sound from all directions, collected from thirty real-world environments. item.title: Agent-Editing World Model: Rethinking World Modeling for LLM Agents
item.description: By Shuang Sun, Guoxin Chen, Fanzhe Meng (Renmin University of China) Agent-Editing World Model, Rethinking World Modeling for LLM Agents. The first three authors are Shuang Sun, Guoxin Chen, and Fanzhe Meng, all from the Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence at Renmin University of China, with the senior authors being Wayne Xin Zhao, Hongteng Xu, and Ji-Rong Wen, the last two being long-time figures in information retrieval and machine learning. The premise of this paper is a reframe of what a world model should actually model for an LLM agent. The standard approach in the literature is to have the world model predict what the environment will observe, essentially simulate the next tool output, the next terminal readout, the next webpage. The authors argue this is the wrong target. Tool responses are high-entropy and execution-dependent, so reconstructing them accurately is expensive, and when the real tool is sitting right there and can just be called, the predicted observation adds little value on top of the ground-truth one. What actually matters, they argue, is whether the agent's next reasoning step and action will move the task forward, or whether it is a noisy detour that will have to be walked back later. That is a different modeling problem, and it is what the Agent-Editing World Model, or AEWM, is built to answer. The paper names the specific failure mode it is targeting: task-state contamination. In a long agent trace, the history accumulates unsupported assumptions, outdated plans, and reasoning that was reasonable at step ten but is wrong at step forty. The model keeps that contaminated context in its window, and it keeps conditioning on it, so the bad state persists and quietly distorts every subsequent decision. item.title: Qwen-Planner-Agent: A Closed-Loop AI-for-AI Framework for Real-World Mobile Planner Agents
item.description: By Tingyu Qu, Weigao Sun, Yuecheng Liu (Alibaba Token Hub) Qwen-Planner-Agent, A Closed-Loop AI-for-AI Framework for Real-World Mobile Planner Agents. The first three authors are Tingyu Qu, Weigao Sun, and Yuecheng Liu, from the MAI Team at Alibaba's Token Hub, with the remaining authors including Junpeng Zhao, Long Chen, and Steven Hoi. The question the paper asks is the one that has been sitting under every agent-building discussion for a year: can AI be both the thing being built and the thing doing the building? Not in some narrow benchmark sense, but in the full loop, where models construct the training tasks, generate the training data, evaluate the model they just trained, and then propose what to change for the next round. The phrase AI-for-AI has become a marketing term, applied to anything from a data-generation pipeline to a single prompt-optimization loop, so the bar for taking a paper that uses it seriously is high, and this paper meets it by building the whole loop rather than describing it. The testbed it picks is one of the hardest available: a mobile phone planner. A planner agent is the top of the stack, the model that decomposes a user goal into a sequence of lower-level actions, manages memory, routes to tools, and decides when a sub-task is done. Real-device interaction is slow and expensive, mobile tasks are long-horizon and messy, and the environment, the actual phones, do not reset cleanly between runs, which makes every piece of the loop harder than it would be in a sandbox. Choosing mobile as the proving ground is the right choice for this kind of paper, because a closed loop that only works in a resettable sandbox says very little about whether the loop can survive a production environment.

item.title: IterSynth: Rethinking Deep Search Agents via Role-Decoupled Iterative Synthesis
item.description: By Xingyu Wu, Yuchen Yan, Zhengxi Lu (Zhejiang University, Tencent) IterSynth, Rethinking Deep Search Agents via Role-Decoupled Iterative Synthesis. The first three authors are Xingyu Wu, Yuchen Yan, and Zhengxi Lu, with the team spanning Zhejiang University and Tencent, and Yongliang Shen of Zhejiang University as the corresponding author. This paper is about the shape of the loop, not the size of the model, which is what makes it worth a slot. Every open-weight deep search agent out there, the ones that imitate Deep Research and the like, runs a ReAct-style loop: one policy, one ever-growing context, interleaving think, search, read, think, search, read, until it emits an answer. The authors identify two structural problems with that shape, and then measure one of them in a way that is harder to argue with. The first problem is role coupling: a single policy is doing planning, query formulation, evidence filtering, conflict resolution, and final synthesis all at once, and the paper's claim is that one undifferentiated policy is bad at being all of those things simultaneously. The second problem is context accumulation: the search history keeps growing, noise piles on signal, and early mistakes propagate forward. And here is the measurement. They take two strong frontier backbones, DeepSeek and Claude Sonnet, run them under a standard ReAct deep search agent with a generous sixty-four kilotoken context, and count how often the trajectory simply runs out of context before it ever reaches an answer. On the hardest benchmark, a hundred-question subset of BrowseComp, the non-completion rate is between fifty-nine and sixty-five percent. That is not a small-model failure. That is the architecture failing, even with frontier models driving it.

item.title: AgentKernel: The Trust-Native Agentic Operating System
item.description: By Zhenhua Zou, Sheng Guo, Qiuyang Zhan (DeepKernel Lab, Tsinghua University) AgentKernel, The Trust-Native Agentic Operating System. A paper from the DeepKernel Lab, the first three authors are Zhenhua Zou, Sheng Guo, and Qiuyang Zhan, with Zhuotao Liu of Tsinghua University as the corresponding author. Read with the right expectations, this is a sharp piece of work. Read with the wrong ones, it is a position paper with no numbers, and I want to be clear up front which it is: there is no implementation, no benchmark, no threat-model evaluation. It is an architecture and a set of design principles, presented with the confidence of a manifesto. What it does well is name a real gap, and it names it better than most. The gap is this. Every serious agent stack in production, the coding agents inside your IDE, the open harnesses, the enterprise orchestration frameworks, is an LLM fused with multi-source context and high-privilege tools. And all of them share the same structural property: there is no OS underneath. Classical applications were born into a world with process isolation, virtual memory, mandatory access control, provenance. Agents operate in what the paper calls an infrastructural vacuum: identity is a self-declared string, perception is unmediated, memory has no provenance discipline, and tool permissions are vague and slow-changing. The paper's central claim, and the one I find most defensible, is that this is not just a security gap, it is a capability gap. The same missing substrate that blocks trustworthy deployment is what caps how much autonomy you can safely grant. You cannot grant an agent broad tool privileges if the boundary is a prompt-level guardrail, because the boundary is bypassable by construction, and a bypassable boundary means you have to grant narrow privileges, which means the agent is weak.

item.title: The Past Frames the Future: Memory for Autoregressive Video Generation
item.description: By Harold Haodong Chen, Rongjin Guo, Disen Lan (HKUST, Carnegie Mellon University, New York University, NVIDIA) The Past Frames the Future: Memory for Autoregressive Video Generation. The first three authors are Harold Haodong Chen, Rongjin Guo, and Disen Lan, from HKUST, Carnegie Mellon University, and New York University, among a roster that runs to twenty-five people with core supervisors at NVIDIA and elsewhere. Autoregressive video generation extends a clip one step at a time: predict the next frame or chunk from everything generated so far, append it, repeat. It is the natural paradigm for anything long-horizon, interactive, or open-ended, and for a few years it looked like the only serious route to video that goes on forever. Then the field ran into its fundamental bottleneck, and this survey is an attempt to organize the response to it. The bottleneck is memory in the strictest sense. A practical model has a bounded context window, bounded storage, and bounded compute. Critical historical information, the identity of a character, the layout of a room, the state of an object after it was knocked over, the consequences of an intervention, routinely leaves the active context long before it stops mattering. The survey's operational definition is clean: a state functions as memory when its removal or modification changes later outputs, even after the originating evidence is no longer locally available. Note what that definition does not do. It does not draw a line between memory and long context. Recent tokens densely consumed at every step are active context; as information is selectively retained, compressed, retrieved, consolidated, or revised beyond the local window, it becomes memory. The boundary is functional, not a window size, which is the right call, because the field has been using the word memory for mechanisms that differ enormously.

item.title: HappyWorld-Bench
item.description: By Zhiqi Bai, Junai Cai, Yixin Chen (Alibaba, Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence, Tsinghua University, Peking University) HappyWorld-Bench. The first three authors, in alphabetical order, are Zhiqi Bai, Junai Cai, and Yixin Chen, from Alibaba's Token Hub, the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence, and Tsinghua University, with the full roster of thirty-seven spanning Peking University and Nanjing University as well. The premise is simple and the current state of the art is uncomfortable: a world model is only as useful as its predictions are under interaction. Photorealistic frames are the easy part. The hard requirement is that the world stays geometrically consistent when the camera moves, physically plausible when you touch it, persistent over long rollouts and revisits, and responsive when you intervene, change a rule, or apply a force. The complaint this paper is aimed at is fragmentation. Video world model benchmarks, spatial scene benchmarks, and embodied interaction benchmarks have each developed their own protocols, and none of them share a capability vocabulary, so you cannot tell whether a model that tops one leaderboard is actually a better world model or just a better video generator. HappyWorld-Bench's answer is a shared hierarchy, six levels they call W1 through W6, from the Perceptual World, coherent generation from a condition, through Interactive and Persistent World, where actions produce state transitions and state survives occlusion and revisits, up to Programmable World, where natural-language interventions must change only what they target, and Scalable and Universal World, shared multi-agent environments and full real-world replication. The levels are a ladder of what a world model owes the agent, and the benchmark instantiates that ladder across three separate tracks, each matched to a model family.

item.title: RewardVerse: Rubric-Guided Policy Optimization for Video Reward Modeling
item.description: By Zhenchen Tang, Yang Li, Songlin Yang (Chinese Academy of Sciences, Tencent, HKUST) RewardVerse: Rubric-Guided Policy Optimization for Video Reward Modeling. The first three authors are Zhenchen Tang, Yang Li, and Songlin Yang, from the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Tencent, and the University of Science and Technology in Hong Kong, with the corresponding author Jing Dong and project lead Songlin Yang. Reinforcement learning is now how video generation models get aligned to human taste, and the reward model is the whole ballgame, because everything downstream optimizes against whatever number it emits. The problem the authors name is scalar drift. Most video reward models take a video and map it directly to a single scalar score, either by regression or by a reasoning chain that ends in a number. But video quality is subjective and multi-dimensional, and with no explicit criteria anchoring the score, the scoring scale collapses into a narrow band or shifts whenever the prompt or context changes. The reward, which is supposed to be a stable training signal, becomes unstable exactly when the RL loop needs it most. The fix borrows from how professional human annotators actually work: nobody scores a video cold. They first break the evaluation into explicit criteria, then score against those criteria. RewardVerse makes that intermediate step explicit and learnable. The architecture inserts a dynamic rubric between the evaluation query and the scorer. Given a query, which pairs an evaluation dimension, say logic, with the actual prompt, a rubric generator first writes out explicit evaluation criteria, each with a theme, a weight, and a hint, for example check that the eyelines stay consistent across the cut. item.title: Spatial-Interactor: Learning Spatial Reasoning through Interaction with the Observable Physical World
item.description: By Kaixiang Yao, Xu Wang, Miao Pan (Zhejiang University, SAP) Spatial-Interactor: Learning Spatial Reasoning through Interaction with the Observable Physical World. The first three authors, two of them equal contributors, are Kaixiang Yao, Xu Wang, and Miao Pan, from the OmniAI Group at Zhejiang University, with Weishi Wang and Daniel Dahlmeier from SAP and the rest of the roster at Zhejiang. The diagnosis comes first, and it is two sharp little experiments. The first is a frame-shuffling diagnostic. Take a video spatial reasoning benchmark, sample thirty-two frames from each video, and randomly shuffle their order before showing them to the model. If a model actually understands how the scene evolves over time, shuffling the temporal order should hurt it badly. It barely does: Qwen's three-billion and seven-billion vision-language models drop by only zero point nine and zero point eight points, with no subtask moving more than one point four. The models are not modeling temporal transitions at all; they are reading order-invariant visual cues, basically describing the scene and pattern-matching. The second experiment separates local perception from long-horizon integration. On a local interaction task, the seven-billion model scores fifty-four point seven. On a long-horizon camera-displacement task, which requires accumulating motion information across the whole trajectory, the same model collapses to eight point six. Even a frontier model, GPT-5.5, drops from eighty-eight point seven to twenty-three point nine. And when the authors feed GPT-5.5 its own generated descriptions of the local state transitions between consecutive segments as extra text, its camera-displacement score climbs back up from twenty-three point nine to thirty-five point five. item.title: SpeakerMem-R1: Speaker-Centered Dual-Track Memory for Multi-Party Dialogue
item.description: By Haobo Zheng, Tan Tang, Yan Chen (Zhejiang University) SpeakerMem-R1: Speaker-Centered Dual-Track Memory for Multi-Party Dialogue. The first three authors are Haobo Zheng, Tan Tang, and Yan Chen, from the State Key Laboratory of CAD and CG at Zhejiang University, with the remaining authors Weijie Wang and Yingcai Wu. Most long-term memory work for language models is built around one user and one assistant: split the conversation, compress it, index it by relevance, retrieve the relevant chunk at query time. That works until the conversation has more than two people, and it fails in a specific, describable way. A group chat is not a longer version of a two-person chat. It contains speaker relations, who replied to whom, cross-topic branches, and states that get revised over time, and flattening that into a message stream you then compress in order throws away exactly the structure that makes group memory hard. The two bottlenecks the authors isolate are message attribution, distinguishing who said what, whom it is about, and whether a piece of information is private to one person or shared by the group, and state reconstruction, recovering the current or a past state from clues that are distributed across different members, the group as a whole, and different times. A relevance retriever can find the sentence, but it cannot tell you that it was said by the quiet member about a different member, and that it was later walked back.

item.title: PACT: From Credit Assignment to Critic Alignment
item.description: By Jiayan Fu, Hang Xu, Yong Zhang (AllSpark Research) PACT: From Credit Assignment to Critic Alignment. The paper carries the byline AllSpark Research, and the first three listed authors are Jiayan Fu, Hang Xu, and Yong Zhang, with the remaining authors including Zhaokai Luo, Yao Hu, Dongyan Zhao, and Mu Chuan. The problem is the granularity mismatch at the heart of reinforcement learning for language models. The training signal is a scalar outcome reward that arrives only after the whole trajectory is complete, but the optimization happens at the level of individual tokens. So the question that every RL algorithm actually answers, in some implicit and usually algorithm-dependent way, is: how should the final outcome be attributed to the tokens that produced it? That question is credit assignment, and the uncomfortable fact this paper starts from is that credit has no generally accepted mathematical definition. Everyone operationalizes it with a different quantity, and nobody has said what the quantity should be. The authors' move is to define it by its properties. They postulate three regularity conditions: Completeness, the credit over the whole trajectory must sum to the outcome; Prefix Consistency, the credit you assign has to be consistent as the trajectory grows one token at a time; and Neutrality, tokens that do not change the expected outcome should carry no credit. And then they prove these three conditions uniquely determine token-level credit. There is exactly one object that satisfies all three, and that object subsumes the related forms that prior work derived under specific objectives.

item.title: Hunyuan-A13B Technical Report
item.description: By Tencent Hunyuan Team (Tencent) Hunyuan-A13B Technical Report. This is a release from Tencent's Hunyuan team, and the author list is a long roster of seventy-five people, the first three named being Ao Liu, Botong Zhou, and Can Xu, so the honest byline is the team rather than any individual. This is a new foundation model, so it is covered under the standing rule that any paper introducing a new foundation model gets an episode, and it is a real one, not a control layer or a fine-tune. Hunyuan-A13B is an open-source large language model built on a mixture-of-experts architecture. The number in the name is the active count: it has eighty billion total parameters but activates only thirteen billion during inference, which is the classic MoE trade, spend the parameters on capacity but pay only for the active ones at serving time. The design goal stated up front is to balance capability, compute efficiency, and deployment cost, and the whole report is organized around whether a thirteen-billion-active model can punch up into the range of much larger dense models. The pre-training is the part worth reading for a technical audience. They trained on a rigorously filtered corpus of more than twenty trillion tokens, and they put particular emphasis on science, technology, engineering, and math data, building a refined labeling system and a multi-dimensional difficulty-grading framework to select harder, higher-quality STEM content. The stated motivation is that the quality of the STEM data sets the upper bound on reasoning ability, which is a fair claim given that competition math and science reasoning are where the frontier models actually differ. After the main pre-training they run a fast annealing stage to consolidate performance and a long-context stage that scales the window to two hundred fifty six thousand tokens. item.title: Bellman Policy Optimization
item.description: By Zhuoqing Song, Haotian Xu, Xikun Zhang (Apodex US, Inc.; Princeton University) Bellman Policy Optimization. The first three authors are Zhuoqing Song, Haotian Xu, and Xikun Zhang, from Apodex US, Inc., with Song also affiliated with Princeton University. The fourth author is Lidong Bing. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is now the standard recipe for teaching language models to reason: you sample a group of answers to each prompt, let a deterministic verifier score the final answer, and push the policy toward the high-scoring ones. The dominant implementation is GRPO and its variants, which normalize rewards within the group and apply a PPO-style clipped surrogate on token-level importance ratios. The standing complaint against this family of methods is not that it works, it does, it is that the whole apparatus is a patchwork of heuristics. The advantage estimate is a group mean and standard deviation, the clipping bounds are hand-tuned, and the importance ratio between the rollout policy and the training policy is a known source of instability whenever the two drift apart, which in practice is always, because rollout and training run on different engines in mixed precision. This paper starts from a different ancestor. Policy Mirror Descent is an older, theoretically cleaner objective that updates the policy using action values and a KL penalty, and its exact solution is a reweighting of the behavior policy by the exponential of the advantage. item.title: Ovis-Embedding: Pushing the Frontiers of Universal Omni-Modal Embeddings
item.description: By Ovis Team (Ant Group) Ovis-Embedding: Pushing the Frontiers of Universal Omni-Modal Embeddings. The byline is the Ovis Team at Ant Group, and the paper is built on the pretrained Qwen-omni backbone. Multi-modal embedding models have followed a familiar path: you train a model to map text, images, and video into a shared space where similarity means relatedness, and you measure success on retrieval and classification benchmarks. The problem with most of them is that they are not actually omni-modal. They handle text and images, maybe video, but they do not handle audio, and they do not handle the mixture of all four in a single embedding. That means if you want to retrieve a video given a spoken query, or match an image to a description that was transcribed from audio, you are stuck with a system that was never trained to sit at the intersection of all the modalities it is supposed to connect. Ovis-Embedding is a family of models, in multiple sizes, trained to produce a single embedding from any combination of text, image, audio, and video, so that the embedding space is genuinely shared across all four. The training recipe is where the technical contribution sits. They start from the Qwen-omni backbone and use a low-rank adapter, LoRA, initialized at a small rank, rather than fine-tuning the full model, which keeps the pretrained multi-modal representations intact while teaching the model to produce the embedding objective.

item.title: From Pattern Recognizers to Personalized Companions: A Survey of Large Language Models in Mental Health
item.description: By Yuchen Li, Zihan Ma, Yixiang Sun (Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Central South University) From Pattern Recognizers to Personalized Companions: A Survey of Large Language Models in Mental Health. The first three authors are Yuchen Li, Zihan Ma, and Yixiang Sun, from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and the Central South University, with a full team of eleven, including Peng Zhang, Jinfeng Zhou, and Xiang Wan. This is a survey, and it is the kind of survey that earns its place by organizing a field that has been growing without a shared vocabulary. Large language models are being deployed across mental health: as screening tools, as conversational support systems, as therapeutic agents, as data annotators, and as research instruments for studying the language of mental states. But the field's literature is scattered across clinical psychology, computer science, and human-computer interaction, and the same system gets called a chatbot, an AI companion, a digital therapeutic, and a large language model agent depending on which journal it appears in. This survey's contribution is a three-phase taxonomy that maps the field's actual progression. Phase one is pattern recognition: models that classify or detect mental-health conditions from text, the depression-detection-in-social-media line of work, which predates the LLM era and now runs on LLM-based classifiers. Phase two is empathetic conversation: systems that hold a supportive dialogue, detect crisis signals, and respond with clinical-grade empathy, the Woebot and Replika family of products and their academic descendants. Phase three, which the survey argues is where the field is actually heading, is longitudinal personalized companions: stateful agents that maintain a persistent model of a specific user over time, with memory, personalization, and the ability to adapt their interventions as the user changes. item.title: Lean Pool: An AI-Maintained Archive of Formalized Mathematics
item.description: By Vasily Ilin (University of Washington) Lean Pool: An AI-Maintained Archive of Formalized Mathematics. The sole author is Vasily Ilin, from the University of Washington, and there is a detail in the paper that sets the tone for the whole thing: the human-written portion of the manuscript consists of a single page, and the author states plainly that the rest of the paper was produced almost entirely by AI. The motivation is a bottleneck argument. AI systems are now generating mathematical arguments at a rate that exceeds the rate at which mathematicians can read and absorb them, and the fix, which the last year of frontier lab releases has validated, is formalization: you ship the argument with a Lean proof, and the Lean kernel mechanically checks it while the mathematics is still being understood. OpenAI's Ten Advances in mathematics and the finite-time blowup result for Navier-Stokes both shipped this way, long AI-generated arguments with accompanying Lean formalizations. But now the bottleneck moves. Once generation is commodified, verification and reuse become the constraint, and the specific constraint this paper addresses is maintenance. Formal proofs are not static documents. They are compiled code that depends on Mathlib, and Mathlib moves: every Lean or Mathlib release breaks a chunk of downstream code, and a formalization that is not actively re-verified against the current library is a formalization that is slowly rotting. Mathlib itself, the canonical shared library, grows at a roughly linear rate because it is gated by strict human review, and it does not contain the definitions and theorems needed for much of research-level mathematics. item.title: Recursive self-improvement of AI research agents
item.description: By Dhruv Srikanth, Bingchen Zhao, Dixing Xu (Weco AI) Recursive self-improvement of AI research agents. The first three authors are Dhruv Srikanth, Bingchen Zhao, and Dixing Xu, from Weco AI, with co-authors Yuxiang Wu and Zhengyao Jiang at the same company. The premise is a pointed one. AI research agents are already automating pieces of AI R&D: machine learning engineering, GPU kernel optimization, algorithm search, harness design. But notice where the improvement stops: the agents make the artifacts better, while the research process that produces them stays fixed. In conventional R&D, the long-standing empirical trend is that cumulative spending on research yields diminishing returns, so if the process itself never improves, the cost of the next increment keeps climbing. Recursive self-improvement points the process at itself: the agent's own code is the object of optimization, and each accepted rewrite becomes the agent that the next round edits. The paper presents AIDE squared, a two-loop system that runs this at the harness layer, the code around the model that controls an agent's search policy, context management, and verification. The inner loop is a research agent that optimizes code against a measurable metric on a suite of AI R&D tasks under a fixed dollar budget. The outer loop proposes rewrites of the inner agent's code and grades each candidate by running it on a selection benchmark, scoring the resulting solutions on private held-out data that the candidate never sees, and keeping a rewrite only if its aggregate private grade beats the incumbent. The design contains two deliberate anti-gaming measures. First, the inner agent optimizes against public task scores, while the outer loop selects on private held-out grades, so the inner agent cannot directly optimize the selection criterion. item.title: Emergent Collusion in Long-Horizon LLM Agent Interaction
item.description: By Xinrui Shi, Yanzhe Zhang, Diyi Yang (Stanford University, Georgia Institute of Technology) Emergent Collusion in Long-Horizon LLM Agent Interaction. The first three authors are Xinrui Shi, Yanzhe Zhang, and Diyi Yang, from Stanford University and the Georgia Institute of Technology, with the project done while Shi was visiting Stanford. Most multi-agent safety work asks whether agents can be made to misbehave: you give them adversarial instructions, or train an optimizer to elicit covert behavior, and you measure what comes out. This paper asks the quieter, arguably more important question: if you do absolutely nothing malicious, do agents develop undesirable coordination on their own, just from interacting for a long time with shared incentives? The setup is a controlled two-agent environment. Two agents, A and B, play 10-episode trajectories over three task types, each with 50 instances and a verifiable ground truth: code analysis, where the agent tests a Python function for an injected bug; data search, where it writes SQL against a SQLite database to locate rows matching a natural-language query; and record extraction, where it selects records from a document by inclusion and exclusion criteria. Each episode has four phases: each agent independently completes its task, with a complete raw log recorded; they exchange messages over a five-round communication channel; each submits ACCEPT or REJECT on its peer's task; and both receive a shared reward plus feedback, then write a private reflection, with memory carried across episodes. The reward is 10 points per correct verdict, so a perfectly coordinated episode is worth 20. The twist is the verification protocol: a compliant verdict must be based on the peer's complete raw log, and if the log is unavailable, the only compliant verdict is REJECT. item.title: RRSI: Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses
item.description: By Peng Xia, Rujun Han, Zifeng Wang (Google Cloud AI Research, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Stanford University, Washington University in St. Louis) RRSI: Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses. The first three authors are Peng Xia, Rujun Han, and Zifeng Wang, from Google Cloud AI Research, with co-authors at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Stanford University, and Washington University in St. Louis. The lead author did the work as a student researcher at Google Cloud AI Research. The premise is that an LLM agent is a system, not a model. A frozen backbone sits inside a harness: the system prompt, the control flow that decides when to plan, act, reflect, or stop, the tool interfaces, the memory and skill files, and the context management that decides what the policy sees at each step. A lot of recent agent progress has come from editing that harness by hand, and a wave of recent methods automates the loop: run the current harness on a set of evolution tasks, summarize the failures into feedback, have a proposer model draft candidate harnesses, evaluate them, and keep the best one. That is, in practice, recursive self-improvement at the agent-system level. The paper's claim is that this loop has a real failure mode that nobody had cleanly isolated: the evolution overfits to the split it is scored on. The evolve-set score climbs while the gain on unseen benchmarks shrinks or disappears.

item.title: WorldCrafter: Consistent Video World Model with Implicit 3D-aware Memory
item.description: By Wangbo Yu, Kunhao Liu, Wenbo Hu (ARC Lab at Tencent IEG, Peking University) WorldCrafter: Consistent Video World Model with Implicit 3D-aware Memory. The first three authors are Wangbo Yu, Kunhao Liu, and Wenbo Hu, from the ARC Lab at Tencent IEG, with co-authors from Peking University. Video world models generate new observations in response to user actions, turning video generation into interactive simulation. The unsolved part is memory. You walk around a generated scene, turn around, and walk back: the scene you already saw should still be there, unchanged, but seen from a new angle. Current models struggle with this over long horizons and across viewpoints. The straightforward fix is to feed previously generated frames back into attention, but full-history attention is prohibitively expensive, and selective retrieval trades coverage for efficiency. Explicit spatial memories, like reconstructed 3D geometry, give you a shared reference but depend on accurate geometry and fall apart on dynamic scenes. Implicit memories compress history into learned representations, but the geometry-oriented ones optimize for geometric prediction rather than for the appearance fidelity you need to actually reproduce a previously seen scene. Their answer is to build the memory from a pretrained 3D scene-representation encoder and co-train it with the video generator. The key design decision is the readout. They compare two ways of turning the accumulated history into something the denoiser can use: pose-free readout, which just aggregates what has been seen, and pose-guided readout, where the camera pose you are about to render from shapes how the multi-view evidence is compressed. The insight is that the video generator has a limited token budget for conditioning, and what matters in that budget is the information relevant to the viewpoint you are currently requesting, not an undi

item.title: Transferring the Intelligence of VLMs to Robotic Control
item.description: By Meng-Hao Guo, Zhe-Han Mo, Jia-Jun Wang (Tsinghua University, Tencent Hunyuan) RoboDawn, from Meng-Hao Guo and Zhe-Han Mo of Tsinghua University and colleagues at Tencent Hunyuan, asks a question that has been implicit in the whole vision-language-action literature but never quite tested this directly: can a pretrained vision-language model, with its parameters completely frozen, be dropped into closed-loop robotic control and actually work, using nothing but a well-designed action interface and a handful of in-context demonstrations? The answer they report is yes, and by a wide margin. Across 87 manipulation tasks, their zero-shot agentic system beats state-of-the-art end-to-end vision-language-action models by up to 31.8 percentage points on average success rate, and it transfers across embodiments and environments without any task-specific training. The setup is worth stating precisely. An end-to-end VLA model, the dominant paradigm in robot learning, takes a pretrained VLM and adapts it, usually with massive amounts of action data, into a policy that directly predicts executable robot actions from observations. The entire field assumes the adaptation is necessary. RoboDawn instead treats the VLM as a frozen oracle and builds everything else around it. The system has three components. First, a human-intuitive action interface: instead of exposing raw joint torques or low-level controller states, the VLM issues semantic commands in a small, readable syntax, like left move x plus ten, left rotate yaw minus thirty, left gripper close. The key design choice is the gripper interaction point, the midpoint between the two fingertips, which is used consistently for visual annotations, state reporting, and motion commands, so the model always reasons about the point actually touching the object rather than the wrist pose the controller tracks. item.title: GameHorizon Suite: Multi-Horizon Data and Evaluation in Gameplay
item.description: By Yiran Wang, Xingyilang Yin, Junfu Pu (ARC Lab at Tencent, Great Bay University, National University of Singapore, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, CUHK, University of Macau) GameHorizon Suite: Multi-Horizon Data and Evaluation in Gameplay. The first three authors are Yiran Wang, Xingyilang Yin, and Junfu Pu, from the ARC Lab at Tencent, with co-authors at Great Bay University, the National University of Singapore, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, CUHK, and the University of Macau. The motivation is a measurement gap. Video games are a legitimate testbed for AI because a single game exercises visual understanding, instruction decomposition, goal planning, and precise action control all at once, and the objectives naturally span temporal horizons: grab an item in a few seconds, win a fight over a few minutes, execute a strategy that unfolds across a session. But the field has split into two model families that are never measured together. Dedicated game agents, built as lightweight vision-language-action policies, are optimized for high-frequency acting and have no capacity to plan. General-purpose vision-language models and computer-use agents are strong at planning, but their action execution has never been systematically measured; the few reported cases, like frontier models playing Pokemon, run on bespoke harnesses that cannot be compared across models. Everything in between is either confined to one game, or to Minecraft, or to mini-games; it lacks language instruction annotations; and its online evaluation runs three to twenty rollouts per model, which is statistically meaningless.

item.title: VideoGen-Agent: Reinforcing Video Generation Agents
item.description: By Binxu Li, Haoyi Duan, Yuhui Zhang (Princeton University, Stanford University, UC Davis) VideoGen-Agent, from Binxu Li, Haoyi Duan, and Yuhui Zhang of Princeton University with colleagues at Stanford, UC Davis, and CUHK's MMLab, is a clean demonstration of a pattern the agent community keeps rediscovering, applied to video: the generation model does not need to be better, it needs to be wrapped. Their agent is trained with multitask agentic reinforcement learning to use external tools when generating video, coordinating augmentation, generation, and verification tools across multiple turns, and it improves its own base text-to-video generator by 19.1 points on their new benchmark, from 56.5 to 75.6. The second result is the one I would actually remember: when they upgrade the generation tools underneath the trained agent, with no additional agent training, the score rises to 86.1. The agent's learned policy is a substrate that future generator improvements flow through. The motivation is the known gap between video visual quality and video correctness. Modern diffusion-based video models make photorealistic, temporally coherent footage, but they generate content only from what they absorbed in pretraining, which produces a specific taxonomy of failure: named techniques depicted wrong, a person's identity drifting across a clip, motion violating gravity or collision physics, and ordered sequences of actions getting phases dropped or reordered. Each failure maps to a tool. Procedural knowledge problems want web or image search to ground the technique. Identity preservation wants retrieved reference images of the specific person or character. item.title: OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching
item.description: By Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Meiyi Qiang (Peking University, University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Zhongguancun Academy) OmniEdu, from Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, and Meiyi Qiang of Peking University with colleagues at the University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Zhongguancun Academy, is a new open model family, and this is the episode where the standing rule matters: any paper that introduces a new foundation model gets covered, and OmniEdu qualifies. It is a family of open K-12 foundation models at three sizes, 4B, 9B, and 27B, fine-tuned from Qwen 3.5 base models with a capability-oriented instruction-tuning corpus, and the contribution is the data pipeline and the capability taxonomy as much as the weights. The 27B model reaches 63.12 percent exact match and 76.69 percent F1 on K12-Bench, 85.89 percent on MathFish, 86.95 percent on EDUMATH, 78.74 percent on the scaffold setting of MathTutorBench, and the best teaching average of 3.02 on LongTutor among the models they evaluate. The framing is a taxonomy. Educational language models tend to specialize: some solve problems well, some can tutor, but training mixtures are usually organized by source or by task, and the four capabilities a useful educational system needs get muddled together. OmniEdu organizes supervision around four explicit capabilities. Subject competence, actually solving K-12 problems in mathematics, science, and reading. Curriculum grounding, understanding how knowledge is structured in official textbooks and standards, which is what lets a model say this topic comes after that one in the grade level. Diagnostic reasoning, recognizing where a student is actually failing rather than just grading the answer. item.title: Grounded Skill Synthesis from Code at Scale for Agentic Intelligence
item.description: By Yongqi Tong, Pan Wang, Hang Wang (Ant International) Grounded Skill Synthesis from Code at Scale for Agentic Intelligence. The first three authors are Yongqi Tong, Pan Wang, and Hang Wang, all from Ant International, with the remaining authors Jianshe Li, Xin Zhang, Jiang-Ming Yang, and Wei Wu also at the same institution. The paper tackles skill synthesis for agentic systems, meaning the process of turning reusable procedural knowledge into records that an agent can retrieve at inference time and execute. The motivation is that most agents today rediscover the same procedures from scratch, task by task: how to structure a stateful CLI tool, how to handle a retry with backoff, how to validate a configuration before loading it. If those procedures were captured once, verified, and indexed, a new agent could start from them instead of from zero. Two existing routes have known weaknesses. Trajectory-based synthesis distills skills from the agent's own execution traces, which couples every skill to the specific model, tools, and task distribution that produced the trace, and caps skill quality at the generating agent's competence. Document-based synthesis pulls skills from human-written text, which avoids the trajectory coupling but has no executable evidence against which a synthesized procedure can be grounded or verified. The proposal here is a third substrate: source code itself. Code requires no prior agent experience, and it comes with executable evidence. The pipeline is called Code2Skill, and the resulting skill bank, CodeSkillBank, contains just over 1 million accepted records, 1,006,822 to be exact, built from 19,769 popular, actively maintained GitHub repositories.

item.title: EvoOntology: A Self-Evolving Ontology Layer for Data Agents
item.description: By Meiduo Chong, Shaolei Zhang, Ju Fan (Renmin University of China) EvoOntology: A Self-Evolving Ontology Layer for Data Agents. The first three authors are Meiduo Chong, Shaolei Zhang, and Ju Fan, all from Renmin University of China, with the fourth author, Xiaoyong Du, also at the same institution. The paper starts from a problem anyone who has run a text-to-SQL agent over a real database will recognize. A data agent that answers natural-language questions over heterogeneous data, meaning databases, CSV files, and documents at once, has no prior knowledge of what that data looks like. It can only reach it through generic tools, a SQL interface, a file reader, a query API. So it has to probe blindly: issue exploratory queries, guess where a concept lives, inspect irrelevant rows, and start over for the next task. The authors call this the agent-data gap. Their proposal is an intermediate layer, an ontology, that sits between the agent and the raw sources and represents domain concepts, how those concepts map onto physical tables, and the business rules that govern them. The key twist is that the layer is not authored by a human and not injected into the prompt. It is built automatically and then continuously revised, and it is exposed to the agent as an MCP server rather than as a blob of context. The ontology state has three components, kept in a versioned graph. The schema layer defines object types and reference rules, so the agent knows what kinds of entities exist and how they relate. The content layer stores the actual domain knowledge: terms with their meanings, mappings from semantic concepts to exact fields, constraints like how revenue is defined, and evidence entries that record which observed data supported each claim. item.title: RecreationWorld: Scalable and Verifiable Environments for Hybrid Computer-Use Agents
item.description: By Shuai Bai, Jiayong Deng, Yikun Fu (Alibaba Token Hub, Alibaba Group) RecreationWorld: Scalable and Verifiable Environments for Hybrid Computer-Use Agents. The first three authors are Shuai Bai, Jiayong Deng, and Yikun Fu, from Alibaba Token Hub at Alibaba Group, with 29 additional authors at the same institution. Computer-use agents have developed along two separate lines that mostly ignore each other. One line operates applications through the graphical interface, perceiving screens and issuing clicks and keystrokes. The other works through code and the command line, writing and running programs and driving the system through a terminal. A GUI-only agent can watch how a running system behaves but rarely builds the software behind it; a terminal-only agent can author programs but cannot see the interface its actions produce. Real digital work interleaves the two: you operate an application, discover something, then edit the code that drives it, run it, and look at the result. The paper calls agents that sustain that fusion hybrid computer-use agents, and it argues the capability is under-measured because existing benchmarks emphasize one interaction mode or the other. The framework, RecreationWorld, is built around a single task: application recreation. Given a running reference application, the agent must discover its behavior and build a faithful implementation, with no prescribed workflow. The task has three parts. The input is a high-level prompt, interactive access to the running reference, and an environment with both GUI control and software-development tools. The interaction is open: the agent may move freely among operating the reference, writing code, building and launching its own implementation, and visually checking the running candidate against what it observed. item.title: CodeMidas: Scaling Agentic Coding RL Environments from Code Itself
item.description: By Bowen Ye, Lei Li, Shicheng Li (Xiaomi LLM Core; Peking University; University of Hong Kong; Renmin University of China) CodeMidas: Scaling Agentic Coding RL Environments from Code Itself. The first three authors are Bowen Ye, Lei Li, and Shicheng Li, from Xiaomi's LLM Core team, with the remaining authors spread across Peking University, the University of Hong Kong, and Renmin University of China. Reinforcement learning for coding agents has two requirements that are easy to state and hard to satisfy: diverse tasks, so the policy generalizes, and reliable reward signals, so the reinforced work is actually correct. Most existing pipelines build RL environments from development artifacts, issues, pull requests, commits, existing tests, or documentation. That works, but it ties the supply of tasks to the coverage of recorded changes, tests, and docs, which caps how far the environment can scale. The proposal here is to use the source code itself as the only task-specific input. Implemented functionality is both the basis of a task and a candidate solution: its public interfaces define what an agent should implement, executing the original code gives you the expected behavior for building tests, and the surrounding codebase becomes a realistic development starting point. The pipeline, CodeMidas, turns that idea into 5,545 training tasks from 3,185 open-source codebases, spanning 23 programming languages and 15 technical domains. Python, TypeScript, and Go are the most represented languages at 21.4, 18.3, and 16.2 percent respectively, and systems software, web technologies, and developer tools are the largest domains. The reference patches are nontrivial: the median solution is 142 lines of added or removed source, with an interquartile range of 66 to 305.

item.title: Paint-Anything: Unified Any-Color Control for Image Generation and Editing
item.description: By Ji Xie, Dewei Zhou, Xinyu Huang (ByteDance Seed; Zhejiang University; Nanjing University) Paint-Anything: Unified Any-Color Control for Image Generation and Editing. The first three authors are Ji Xie, Dewei Zhou, and Xinyu Huang, from ByteDance Seed, with Zhennan Chen and Xun Wang completing the author list, spread across ByteDance Seed, Zhejiang University, and Nanjing University. The paper targets a specific professional requirement that generic text-to-image models do not meet: specifying an object's color with an exact 24-bit hex value, not with a named color like blue or red. A brand designer needs the logo in the exact brand blue. A retailer needs product images in the exact red of a new collection. Prior approaches to color control mostly add something to the model: learned color tokens, task-specific modules, numeric color encoders, or training-free inference-time techniques like sampling guidance and attention manipulation. Those designs are hard to scale across the full color space, hard to port to new architectures, or expensive at inference time, and they tend to treat generation, colorization, and editing as separate problems. The starting insight here is simpler: modern language models can already parse hex strings. The paper shows that a compact 4-billion-parameter model, Qwen3-4B, given a raw hex color code, produces a plausible spoken description of the color, so a hex string can serve as a prompt-native interface for color without any dedicated color encoder.

item.title: OmniVBench: A Benchmark and Large-Scale Dataset for Omni Reference-to-Video Generation
item.description: By Wenxue Li, Peiyan Guan, Haoyang Jiang (Tencent Online Video BU; The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) OmniVBench: A Benchmark and Large-Scale Dataset for Omni Reference-to-Video Generation. The first three authors are Wenxue Li, Peiyan Guan, and Haoyang Jiang, from Tencent's Online Video BU and The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology in Guangzhou, with the remaining co-authors at the same two institutions. Reference-to-video generation, where a visual reference steers what a video model synthesizes, has moved from simple cases, one object reference for identity, toward compositional settings: the reference might supply content, motion, style, structure, or narrative, and multiple references might have to be combined. The paper calls this emerging paradigm omni reference-to-video, and argues that existing benchmarks do not measure it. They cover a limited range of reference types, they mostly score holistic consistency, whether the reference is "in" the video, and they do not check whether individual reference factors were preserved, disentangled from each other, and routed to the correct target. The paper contributes two artifacts. OmniVBench, a benchmark with 7 task families and 18 fine-grained tasks, 813 evaluation cases, and a factor-grounded evaluation protocol with 12,172 case-specific checklist items. And the Omni-R2V Dataset, 340 thousand processed training samples drawn primarily from a large corpus of professional video footage.

item.title: Reflect, Revise, Reuse: Training-Free Skill Evolution for GUI Agents
item.description: By Bofan Chen, Boxuan Zhang, Fei Tang, Zhengxi Lu, Yong Du, Tongbo Chen, Weiming Lu, Jun Xiao, Yueting Zhuang, Yongliang Shen (Zhejiang University; University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) Reflect, Revise, Reuse: Training-Free Skill Evolution for GUI Agents. The first three authors are Bofan Chen, Boxuan Zhang, and Fei Tang, from Zhejiang University, with the remaining authors spanning Zhejiang University and the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China. The paper tackles a specific failure mode of GUI agents, the systems that operate phone and desktop interfaces on behalf of a user. A GUI agent plans a sequence of clicks and taps, and then the interface moves underneath it. A pop-up appears, a widget relocates, an accessibility tree goes stale, and the plan that was valid thirty seconds ago no longer is. Existing agent-skill frameworks try to handle this by writing reusable procedural knowledge, a skill document the agent consults before acting. But the paper's argument is that most of these skills are static: they are written once, before deployment, and then frozen. The authors' position is that GUI agents do not need better static skills, they need skills that get revised from execution feedback at deployment time, without any additional training. Their proposed system is EvoSkill-GUI, a training-free self-evolving framework built around a reflect, revise, reuse loop. The central design object is the skill package, and it is deliberately structured. Instead of one long document where planning steps, localization hints, and recovery rules are all tangled together, each skill is a multi-file package with separate components: retrieval metadata that says when the skill applies, an executable plan, backup localization strategies for when a selector fails, failure-recovery rules, accessibility utilities, and a record of failure cases. item.title: When2Think: Learning Difficulty-Aware Length Control for Efficient Hybrid Reasoning Models
item.description: By Jaejun Shim, HyunJin Kim, Young Jin Kim, JinYeong Bak (Sungkyunkwan University; Microsoft) When2Think: Learning Difficulty-Aware Length Control for Efficient Hybrid Reasoning Models. The first three authors are Jaejun Shim, HyunJin Kim, and Young Jin Kim, from Sungkyunkwan University and Microsoft, with the final author JinYeong Bak at Sungkyunkwan University. The paper addresses a well-documented inefficiency in large reasoning models, the systems that generate long chains of thought before answering. These models are strong on hard problems, but they do not adapt their effort to the problem in front of them. They overthink easy problems, burning hundreds of reasoning tokens on a question that needed a one-line answer, and they underthink hard ones, terminating the chain too early or producing a fragmented argument. The existing fixes come in two flavors, and both have a cost. A uniform length penalty, a reward that just punishes long outputs, cuts the token budget everywhere, including on the hard problems where the length is doing real work. Rigid routing, deciding in advance whether a problem gets the fast path or the slow path, commits before the model has actually seen how hard the instance is. The authors' formulation is that efficient reasoning is an instance-adaptive computation allocation problem: the right amount of thinking depends on the specific instance, and the model should learn to allocate it.

item.title: What Does Privileged Information Add to On-Policy Self-Distillation?
item.description: By XiuYu Zhang, Wei Chow, Junfeng Fang, Zhenkai Liang, Tat-Seng Chua (National University of Singapore) What Does Privileged Information Add to On-Policy Self-Distillation? The first three authors are XiuYu Zhang, Wei Chow, and Junfeng Fang, from the National University of Singapore, with the remaining authors Zhenkai Liang and Tat-Seng Chua also at the National University of Singapore. The paper asks a deceptively simple question about on-policy self-distillation, a training recipe in which a language model learns from a frozen copy of itself that can see extra information, like the answer to a problem or a worked solution. Giving the teacher model this privileged information seems obviously useful, the teacher can now point the student toward the right answer. But the paper's question is how much of the student's improvement actually comes from that privileged information, and how much comes from the distillation process itself, the simple act of a student being trained to match a teacher that scores its own rollouts. To separate the two, the authors need a design where the answer information is held fixed while everything else varies, and that design is the main contribution. The construction is a reusable suite called AMPLE-MATH, which stands for Answer-Matched Privileged Levels of Explanation. It is built from OpenThoughts, and it contains 5,319 mathematical problems, each with six reasoning views that all share the same verified answer but differ in how much reasoning is exposed. The six views range from answer only, thirteen tokens on average, up through a gist at 76 tokens, key points at 284, a clean solution at 526, a summary at 841, and the full trace at 4,916 tokens. item.title: Region-Level Policy Optimization for Fine-grained MLLM Perception
item.description: By Yuheng Shi, Xiaohuan Pei, Minjing Dong, Chang Xu (University of Sydney; City University of Hong Kong) Region-Level Policy Optimization for Fine-grained MLLM Perception. The first three authors are Yuheng Shi, Xiaohuan Pei, and Minjing Dong, from the University of Sydney and the City University of Hong Kong, with the final author Chang Xu at the University of Sydney. The paper addresses the cost of fine-grained visual perception in multimodal large language models, the systems that answer questions about specific details in an image. The standard fix for fine-grained perception is to raise the input resolution, but higher resolution means more visual tokens, which inflates both the vision-encoding cost and the language-model prefill cost, and answer-relevant evidence often occupies only a small fraction of the image. The paper's starting observation is that fine-grained perception involves two distinct operations, localizing the region of interest and then recognizing its content, and that these two operations have different resolution requirements. The method that follows from that observation is called Vision-RL2, a region-level reinforcement learning approach that optimizes a region proposal network with a signal that standard training cannot provide. The key piece of evidence is a controlled diagnostic built on ZoomBench with Qwen3.5-4B. The model predicts a region of interest box from the scene and then answers from the resulting crop, with the crop capped at at most 128 visual tokens. On a filtered set of cases that the pipeline answers correctly at full resolution and that are not solvable from the question alone, the authors run two sweeps. In the localization sweep, they compress only the scene from which the box is re-predicted, leaving the crop untouched. In the recognition sweep, they freeze the box and compress its crop. item.title: HypoEvolve: Genetic Algorithms Enable Multi-Agent LLMs to Discover Scientific Hypotheses
item.description: By Jieyuan Liu, Mengzhou Hu, Jefferson Chen, JungHo Kong, Pratibha Jagannatha, Yiming Gao, Dexter Pratt, Hsin-Yuan Lee, Zhiting Hu, Trey Ideker, Wei Wang, Eric P. Xing, Zhen Wang (University of California San Diego; Texas A&M University; Carnegie Mellon University; Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence) HypoEvolve: Genetic Algorithms Enable Multi-Agent LLMs to Discover Scientific Hypotheses. The first three authors are Jieyuan Liu, Mengzhou Hu, and Jefferson Chen, from the University of California San Diego, with the remaining authors spanning UC San Diego, Texas A and M University, Carnegie Mellon University, and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence. The paper addresses a question that has become urgent as scientific agents get better: how does the design of collaboration between agents affect the quality of the hypotheses they develop? Recent systems combine scientific agents with evolutionary search, cycling through critique, comparison, and revision. But when such a system performs well, it is impossible to tell how much of the performance comes from the agents' scientific capabilities and how much comes from the rules that direct their collaboration. The paper's contribution is a framework that separates those two things. It makes collaboration an experimental variable: the scientific roles, the prompts, and the evaluation criteria are held fixed, and only the search rules, the rules for combining, revising, and retaining hypotheses, are varied. Hypothesis quality is the measured outcome.

item.title: Score Centering Stabilizes Off-policy Reinforcement Learning
item.description: By Martin Marek, Max Ryabinin (Together AI) Score Centering Stabilizes Off-policy Reinforcement Learning, by Martin Marek and Max Ryabinin of Together AI. If you train language models with reinforcement learning today, you live with an uncomfortable secret: the policy gradient identity that justifies your entire loss only holds if the engine that generates your rollouts and the engine that computes your gradients produce bit-identical outputs. In practice they never do. Training clusters roll out samples on quantized, continuously batched inference engines running asynchronous checkpoints, while gradients flow through a trainer in a different precision with different kernel orderings. Every one of these small differences between the sampler and the trainer is collectively called the training-inference mismatch, and under enough of it, RL runs collapse outright. The standard playbook is importance sampling: reweight every token by the ratio between what the trainer believes and what the sampler believed, usually clipped or masked because raw ratios explode on rare tokens. This paper argues that most of that machinery is aimed at the wrong target. The instability is driven by drift, a bias term in the update that accumulates step after step exactly because the sampler is a moving biased copy of the trainer, and it can be canceled with an additive correction that involves no ratios, no clipping, and no masking.

item.title: SoL-Pi: Recursively Scaling Auto-Research Loops for Efficient Agent Harness
item.description: By Haozhe Liu, Tian Ye, Sensen Gao (NVIDIA; Nanyang Technological University; MIT) SoL-Pi: Recursively Scaling Auto-Research Loops for Efficient Agent Harness. The first three authors are Haozhe Liu, Tian Ye, and Sensen Gao, from NVIDIA, Nanyang Technological University, and MIT. The paper tackles a systems problem that has been quietly getting worse as coding agents move from supervised code completion to unattended, around-the-clock exploration. Once an agent runs long trajectories of reasoning, tool use, and feedback, token efficiency stops being a nice-to-have and becomes a first-order cost concern. Most efficiency work so far has aimed at the model or the infrastructure: faster attention kernels, quantization, cheaper substitute models. The authors take an orthogonal direction. They hold the underlying model fixed and instead optimize the harness, the software layer that mediates every interaction between the model and its environment. The twist is that they do not hand-tune that harness. They let an AI optimizer discover it, using a recursive-self-improvement-inspired search, and they specifically engineer the search so the improvements it finds transfer to tasks it never saw. That last clause is the whole contribution, and it is worth pausing on, because a recent study the authors cite found that evolved harnesses tend to overfit the tasks used during search and deliver only marginal gains on unseen tasks. So the design is built around three principles. Breadth and depth: a broad pool of hypotheses is generated, then promising candidates are implemented, reviewed, and hardened repeatedly. Independent validation: held-out evidence is only evaluated after a candidate is frozen, and those results never flow back into the search, so a validation failure rejects a candidate instead of being patched into a task-specific solution. item.title: An Empirical Study of Harness Design for Coding Agents
item.description: By Run-Ze Fan, Zihao Zhang, Simin Ma (UMass Amherst; Emory University; UNC Charlotte) An Empirical Study of Harness Design for Coding Agents. The first three authors are Run-Ze Fan, Zihao Zhang, and Simin Ma, from UMass Amherst, Emory University, and UNC Charlotte. Two of them did the work during internships at Zoom Video Communications. The problem is that most coding-agent research evaluates harnesses as monoliths. You pick a whole system, run a benchmark, and get a number, but when one harness beats another you have no idea whether the gain came from the planning scaffold, the tool interface, or the context-management policy. Cross-harness studies make it worse: one the authors cite reports Claude-Opus-4.5 doing best in OpenHands while Claude-Sonnet-4.5 does best in SWE-Agent, which tells you harness preferences vary by model but not which component is responsible. The authors' question is whether individual harness components are generally useful or whether each one's effectiveness depends on model capability, task type, and the context budget. Their answer comes from building a deliberately lightweight harness from scratch. The execution loop is fixed as a ReAct loop: each turn assembles the model input, runs the emitted tool calls in a container, and appends the observation to history. item.description: By DeepSeek-AI, Anyi Xu, B. Li (DeepSeek) DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: Pushing the Limits of KV Cache Compression. The first three authors listed are Anyi Xu, Bangcai Lin, and Bing Xue, from DeepSeek, a DeepSeek-AI paper with an author list of well over five hundred names. This is a foundation-model technical report, and it is aimed at one specific bottleneck: the cost of long-context, input-heavy agentic workloads. The authors' framing is that prior work has cut the cost of long-context computation, but prefill is still expensive, and large KV caches still strain HBM, SSD capacity, and data-transfer bandwidth. Compute, storage, and bandwidth together are what keep deployment costs from falling further, and this model is designed to attack exactly that triple. Checkpoints are released on Hugging Face under the DeepSeek organization, so everything described here is reproducible in principle, which matters for a report like this. The model is a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with a 552 billion parameter backbone and support for contexts up to one million tokens. The headline architectural piece is something called the Causal Encoder-Decoder, or CED. In a CED, the upper half of the layers can directly reuse the key and value cache generated by the lower half, which roughly halves the depth of KV generation during prefill. The effect is asymmetric between the two phases of inference: during decode, 16 billion parameters are activated per token, but during prefill only 8 billion. Since agentic workloads are overwhelmingly prefill-heavy, frequent tool calls each triggering a large prefill, that asymmetry is the economic core of the whole design. The paper states that for a sequence length much larger than the sliding window, CED reduces prefill complexity from the product of sequence length and layer count to roughly half of that.

The problem is that different domains decompose their predictive targets differently. A visual state combines location, object, and transformation. A biological state combines cell identity and response. A physical state combines entities, scales, and dynamical modes. item.title: RetireOPD: Self-Retiring On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
item.description: By Yan Yu, Zhengxi Lu, Yizhou Liu (Zhejiang University; Alibaba Group) RetireOPD: Self-Retiring On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning. The first three authors are Yan Yu, Zhengxi Lu, and Yizhou Liu, from Zhejiang University, with the remaining authors also at Zhejiang University and Alibaba Group. Code is released on GitHub under the ZJU-REAL organization. The starting point is a limitation of reinforcement learning for multi-turn agents. An agent trained with RL receives a single scalar reward per trajectory, which is dense in information only at the very end of a long episode and sparse everywhere else. On-policy distillation, OPD, is the standard remedy: you introduce a self-teacher that has access to privileged task skills, and it produces token-level supervision that the skill-free student can use to internalize those skills. The student learns from dense per-token signals instead of one terminal reward, and it does not need the privileged information at inference time. The paper's premise is that this recipe, taken as-is, is undermined by two findings the authors establish in agentic tasks. First, privileged information alone does not make the teacher reliable: a teacher that has access to extra context does not automatically produce a correct supervision signal, because the extra context does not necessarily translate into better token-level decisions. Second, the benefit of the teacher is stage-dependent: it helps early in training and stops helping, or even hurts, later.

item.description: By Hejia Geng, Zesen Huang, Haoyang Li (AItonomy Foundation; PhAI-Labs) ScienceIDE: Turning World's Scientific Codebase into Agent Learnable Environments. It is a large collaborative effort with well over forty authors, so treat the byline as a consortium rather than a single group. The core problem the authors call the scientific experience bottleneck. Coding agents get to learn because a repository has a compiler, tests, and an acceptance condition, so an action has an observable consequence that can be scored. Scientific code, by contrast, is fragmented across incompatible toolchains, encodes correctness in physical quantities and numerical tolerances rather than pass-or-fail unit tests, and rarely comes with a runnable task definition. The result is that you have the raw material, decades of validated numerical software, but no production infrastructure to turn it into training signal. Existing scientific coding and reproducibility benchmarks can evaluate an agent, but they do not let you scale the experience across many repositories and task families. There is a specific place where this bottleneck is most acute, and the authors use it as their motivating example: porting scientific codes to accelerators. Today that work proceeds one hand-written port at a time, each bound to a specific vendor toolchain, and with double precision used as a default rather than as a derived requirement of the science. item.title: Confidence Comes from Experience: Experiential Confidence Estimation from Reasoning to Agents
item.description: By Caiqi Zhang, Xiaochen Zhu, Chengzu Li (University of Cambridge; Google DeepMind) Confidence Comes from Experience: Experiential Confidence Estimation from Reasoning to Agents. The first three authors are Caiqi Zhang, Xiaochen Zhu, and Chengzu Li, and the work comes out of the University of Cambridge, with one author at Google DeepMind. The motivation is a failure mode you have probably seen in an agent log. A model proposes a fix, runs the tests, sees them pass, and then reports high stated confidence, "tests passed, so I'm confident the fix is correct." But a green test is not the same thing as a correct fix, and the model's verbal confidence is not calibrated to whether it is actually right. The paper's premise is that a model's own stated confidence is a weak signal, and that a much better signal lives in the model's past experience: if you keep a record of similar tasks, with what the model's initial confidence was and whether it ultimately succeeded, you can recalibrate its present confidence against that history. That is the "experiential" part. There is a deeper reason stated confidence is unreliable, and it is worth making explicit because it motivates the whole approach. A model's verbal confidence is produced by the same forward pass that produced the answer, so it is a readout of the model's internal state at the moment of answering, before it has any information about whether the answer was right. It is essentially a prior over the question, conditioned on the question text, not on the outcome. The experiential estimate, by contrast, is a posterior: it is the observed success rate over a set of past episodes that looked like this one, which is a quantity that is actually grounded in realized outcomes rather than in the model's own introspection. item.title: Agora: Git as Shared Memory for Collective AutoResearch
item.description: By Yifan Zhang, Yunheng Zou, Shaokun Zhang (NVIDIA) Agora: Git as Shared Memory for Collective AutoResearch. The first three authors are Yifan Zhang, Yunheng Zou, and Shaokun Zhang, and the work comes out of NVIDIA. It is a systems paper with an unusual experimental subject, a community of autonomous research agents working without a planner. The starting point is a known limitation of autonomous research loops. A single coding agent, in the AutoResearch style, can improve a training setup unattended, and that is well established. Each result, insight, hypothesis, verification, and report is an immutable commit, and the parent edges of the commit say what it builds on. The appeal of using Git specifically, rather than a purpose-built coordination store, is worth stating, because it is a design bet. item.title: Rethinking Critic Learning in PPO: Understanding and Mitigating Value Flattening
item.description: By Yizhuo Li, Jianhao Yan, Yun Luo (Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai AI Laboratory; Westlake University; Nanjing University; Tsinghua University; The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Nanyang Technological University) Rethinking Critic Learning in PPO: Understanding and Mitigating Value Flattening. The first three authors are Yizhuo Li, Jianhao Yan, and Yun Luo, and the work spans Shanghai Jiao Tong University, the Shanghai AI Laboratory, Westlake University, Nanjing University, Tsinghua University, the Chinese University of Hong Kong, and Nanyang Technological University. It is a focused method paper on a specific failure mode in one of the most widely used reinforcement-learning algorithms for language models. The context. In reinforcement learning for large language models, Proximal Policy Optimization commonly uses a critic to estimate state values and reduce the variance of the policy updates. The critic is supposed to tell the policy, at each token of a response, roughly what the expected return is from that point forward, so that the advantage, the return minus the baseline, has lower variance than the raw return alone. The paper uncovers a systematic failure mode in these critics that the authors call Value Flattening. The state values, estimated from multiple Monte Carlo returns, collapse toward a flat function: instead of the critic's value changing meaningfully across the tokens of a response, it ends up nearly constant, so the advantage it induces is weak and the policy updates carry less of the signal they are supposed to carry. The claim is that this is not noise in a particular run, it is a structural tendency of how the critic is trained.
