item.title: MaxKernel: Agentic Kernel Generation for TPUs
item.description: By Shangkun Wang, Nina Cai, Charles Hong (Google, Google DeepMind) MaxKernel: Agentic Kernel Generation for TPUs, by Shangkun Wang, Nina Cai, and Charles Hong, from Google and Google DeepMind. The paper presents a multi-agent system for automating TPU kernel engineering, benchmarked on JAXBench, a suite of 50 diverse kernel tasks built from real workloads of state-of-the-art open-source models, plus production kernels where hand-tuned references exist. The headline numbers: a 1.58 times geometric mean speedup across the full JAXBench workloads, and on the eight production kernels with human-written baselines, a 2.32 times geometric mean speedup for the best agent configuration against 2.02 times for the human hand-tuned code. The framework is released as open source under the accelerator-agents repository. The motivation is that TPU kernel work is painstakingly manual. Accelerator APIs are rigid, memory constraints are strict, compiler errors are opaque, and even functionally correct code needs iterative empirical profiling to reach peak performance. Compiler frameworks like Halide, TVM, and Ansor decouple algorithms from scheduling but still demand domain expertise or expensive evolutionary search. LLM-based approaches help, but standard zero-shot or few-shot generation falls short without real-time compiler feedback and profiling in the loop. The architecture is a shared pool of specialized sub-agents orchestrated three different ways. The sub-agents are: a planning agent that writes a high-level algorithmic optimization plan from the hardware specs and the reference implementation; an implementation agent that translates the plan into valid Pallas code, with an iterative compile-fix loop that interprets compiler feedback and resolves errors before execution; a test synthesis agent that builds test suites and an execution agent that runs them on the target hardware

item.title: LLaDA-Image: Building Strong Image Generators with Fully Open Training Recipes
item.description: By Chuyan Chen, Haoxing Chen, Kun Chen (Inclusion AI) LLaDA-Image: Building Strong Image Generators with Fully Open Training Recipes, by Chuyan Chen, Haoxing Chen, and Kun Chen, from the AGI Research Center at Inclusion AI. This one is here both because it has the day's highest true upvote count and because it lands under the standing rule for foundation-model releases: it is a new image-generation base model trained from scratch, and it ships open, which is the part that makes it worth your time rather than just another leaderboard entry. The framing. The paper pairs two things that do not usually get paired this cleanly. One side is a 6 billion parameter Diffusion Transformer, a DiT, trained from scratch as the generation engine. The other side is a frozen vision-language understanding module built on the LLaDA 2.0 Mini diffusion language model backbone, which supplies the semantic and instruction-following prior. The two are coupled so that the understanding module conditions the generation, rather than the generation model trying to learn its own text comprehension from scratch. The key design decision is about data ordering: instead of leaning heavily on paired image-text data from the very start, the authors first build a strong visual generative prior through image-only pre-training and mid-training, and only then move to paired image-text supervised fine-tuning. The stated motivation is that a model that has already learned to generate plausible images from images alone does not have to burn its capacity learning basic visual structure from scratch on the paired data.

item.title: LatentPress: Context Compression Beyond Text and Vision
item.description: By Zhengze Zhou, Hejian Sang (Cornell University, Iowa State University) LatentPress: Context Compression Beyond Text and Vision, by Zhengze Zhou and Hejian Sang, from Cornell University and Iowa State University. This is a small, focused paper on a specific infrastructure problem, and the idea is a clean one: stop carrying compressed context as human-readable text or as rendered images that have to be decoded, and instead write it directly into a third representation, continuous memory tokens that a frozen language model reads straight through its input-embedding interface. If you are building long-context or agentic systems where you compress history to fit the context window, this is a proposal to compress into the model's own latent space rather than into a format you then have to decode back out. The motivation is that the consumer of compressed context is usually a language model, yet the compressed context is almost always produced in a format meant for a human. You either summarize the history into readable text, or you render it into an image and let the model OCR or decode it. Both routes add a decoding step the model did not ask for, and both lose information in the process. Text summaries are cheap to produce but throw away the fine-grained detail a memory task depends on, and image-based compression is more faithful but pays a decoding cost and inherits the OCR error floor. LatentPress's argument is that if the reader is a model, the writer should write in the model's native representation. So the system writes conversational histories and long documents into continuous memory tokens, and the frozen decoder reads those tokens directly through its input-embedding interface, with no text reconstruction at inference time. The result is a third representation that is neither text nor image, but the internal form the model already speaks.

item.title: Why Gated DeltaNet Survives 4-Bit Quantization: NVFP4 W4A4 for the Recurrent Half of a Hybrid 27B LLM
item.description: By Sergii Kozyrev, Davyd Maiboroda (Minima AI) Why Gated DeltaNet Survives 4-Bit Quantization, by Sergii Kozyrev and Davyd Maiboroda, from Minima AI. This is a short, focused systems paper rather than a model release, and its whole argument rests on one counterintuitive claim: the recurrent half of a hybrid large language model is the easier half to quantize, not the harder half. If you are running hybrid models like Qwen 3.8 27B and you have been hand-tuning which blocks to keep in high precision, the paper says the hand-tuning is backwards. The setup. Hybrid large language models interleave ordinary softmax attention with linear-attention layers such as Gated DeltaNet. Gated DeltaNet keeps a recurrent state that summarizes the whole context in a fixed size, which is what makes it cheap to run over long sequences. The catch that has guided the community so far is that a recurrence is supposed to accumulate error. Every small mistake in the state gets carried forward and compounded over thousands of steps, so people assumed the Gated DeltaNet block, especially its decay gate and its write-strength gate, had to stay in 8-bit or 16-bit precision no matter what. Early community 4-bit quantizations of Qwen 3.8 27B, which has 48 Gated DeltaNet layers and 16 attention layers, all left the Gated DeltaNet block in 8 or 16 bits on exactly that intuition. The decay gate in particular was treated as sacred, on the reasoning that a small bias in the decay rate is a small change every single step, and over 32K steps a small per-step bias becomes a large state drift.

item.title: Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning
item.description: By Heng Wang, Jielin Qiu, Wenting Zhao (Salesforce AI Research, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning, by Heng Wang, Jielin Qiu, and Wenting Zhao, from Salesforce AI Research and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. This is a result that sounds like a joke until you check the numbers: the paper argues that the scoring function at the heart of every KV-cache eviction method contributes almost nothing, and that evicting tokens uniformly at random within each attention head matches the best prior evictor while being much faster to serve. If you have built a KV-cache compressor, this paper is proposing you delete your scorer. The problem. Large language models do their best work on tasks that require extended reasoning, and the way they do it is by generating long chains of thought. Long chains of thought make the KV cache a severe memory bottleneck, because every token the model reasons over stays in the cache and has to be attended to. The standard response in the literature is a shared paradigm: score each cached token by some estimate of how much it will matter later, and keep the top-scoring ones. Methods like SnapKV and VaSE are built on exactly this idea, and they invest real engineering in the scoring function, whether that is an attention-magnitude heuristic, a learned importance estimator, or a redundancy-aware variant. The paper's opening claim is that this selection signal, the whole reason those methods exist, is doing almost no work, and it frames the question as an empirical one that the field has not actually checked: everyone assumes the scorer is the point, but nobody has run the obvious control experiment of evicting at random and measuring the gap.

item.title: Rethinking On-Policy Distillation of Large Language Models II: One Training Example
item.description: By Zixuan Fu, Bingxiang He, Yuxin Zuo (Tsinghua University, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Northeastern University) Rethinking On-Policy Distillation of Large Language Models, Part Two: One Training Example, by Zixuan Fu, Bingxiang He, and Yuxin Zuo, from Tsinghua University, the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, and Northeastern University, with collaborators at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and Johns Hopkins. This is a data-efficiency paper that pushes a familiar training method to its most extreme limit and finds something surprising: on-policy distillation, which is usually run on a full dataset of examples, keeps improving for hundreds of steps when you train it on a single query. The paper's argument is that on-policy distillation is not data-hungry the way supervised fine-tuning is, and that the bottleneck has always been the optimization, not the data. The setup. On-policy distillation, or OPD, combines student-generated rollouts with dense token-level supervision from a stronger teacher. The student produces its own sequences, and the teacher scores each token, so the student is always being corrected on the states it actually visits rather than on a fixed dataset of target sequences. This is the property that separates OPD from ordinary supervised fine-tuning: in SFT the student imitates a fixed set of target trajectories, so the data you give it is exactly the states it will see, but in OPD the student explores its own trajectory distribution and the teacher's supervision lands on states the student would actually visit in deployment. Prior work has studied the algorithmic side of this, the loss, the sampling, the token-level signal, but the paper says the role of the training data itself has been left unclear. item.title: Puffin-World: Scaling a Unified Multimodal Model with Native 3D World States
item.description: By Kang Liao, Yihang Luo, Xiao-Ming Wu (S-Lab, Nanyang Technological University, University of Michigan, Beijing Jiaotong University) Puffin-World: Scaling a Unified Multimodal Model with Native 3D World States, by Kang Liao, Yihang Luo, and Xiao-Ming Wu, from S-Lab at Nanyang Technological University, the University of Michigan, and Beijing Jiaotong University, with collaborators at ACE Robotics. This one is here under the standing rule for foundation-model releases, because it is a new unified multimodal model, a single architecture that does scene and physics understanding, free-viewpoint spatial generation, and 3D world generation and reconstruction, all from one set of weights. It is the kind of base-model release the rule is meant to catch, and it ships open with code, models, and datasets. The central design decision is that the model works in what the paper calls native 3D world states, rather than treating 3D as something you reconstruct as a post-processing step. The framework jointly models three native states: physics, which is a gravity field and a latitude map; geometry, which is depth; and appearance, which is the image itself. On top of those three it uses a unified representation the authors call Omni-Camera, which is meant to support diverse tasks and flexible camera motions within one representation rather than a different parameterization per task. The motivation is that a lot of prior work keeps the 3D understanding, the simulation, and the generation as separate modules that you have to stitch together offline, and the paper's argument is that keeping them native and unified in one model is what lets the same architecture do understanding, generation, and reconstruction coherently.

item.title: StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators
item.description: By Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley (Microsoft Research; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) StudentSim, by Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, and Michel Galley, from Microsoft Research, with co-authors from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. The paper's argument in one line: if you want to train and evaluate adaptive AI tutors, you need a scalable source of per-student feedback, and the way to get it is to train a small language model to be that student. The setting is concrete. An AI tutor is only as good as the feedback it gets about which guidance helps which student, and collecting that feedback from real learners is slow, expensive, and sparse. The authors define two properties a student simulator must have. Behavioral fidelity, which they call F: does the simulator reproduce the student's own responses, including the characteristic mistakes? And guidance responsiveness, which they call R: given the student's wrong response and a tutor's correction, does the simulator update toward the corrected response? The two are deliberately separable. A faithful simulator that ignores guidance is useless for training a tutor; a responsive one that does not start from the student's actual competence is a different student. The prior art splits into three lines, and none of them hits both properties at once. Cognitive-state and behavior-prediction models, like knowledge tracing and human-play move predictors, match learner behavior at the population level but have no input channel for natural-language guidance, so they cannot be a reward for a tutor that talks. LLM-prompted student simulators condition on a textual competence description and converse, which scales, but a thin text description is a weak conditioning channel, and a growing validity-focused literature raises architectural and fidelity concerns about exactly that recipe. item.title: SMELT: Scaling Laws for Compute-Matched MoE Looped Transformers
item.description: By Shaowen Wang, Ge Zhang, Kairong Luo (Tsinghua University; ByteDance Seed; M-A-P; TokenWave.AI) SMELT: Scaling Laws for Compute-Matched MoE Looped Transformers, by Shaowen Wang, Ge Zhang, and Kairong Luo of Tsinghua University, ByteDance Seed, M-A-P, and TokenWave AI, with further authors from those labs. Looped transformers repeat a shared block of layers instead of stacking new ones, and the pitch is seductive: reasoning depth without extra parameters, with looped models matching or beating unlooped models several times their size on arithmetic and math. But there is a catch the literature mostly waves away: looping a twelve-layer model to twenty-four executed layers stores half the weights yet spends roughly a twenty-four-layer model's compute per token and needs its full key-value cache. Most prior evaluations hold parameter count fixed and let compute float, so the reported gains conflate an architectural advantage with uncontrolled extra computation. This paper is, by its own accounting, the first multi-scale study to hold all three budgets fixed at once, per-token FLOPs, total non-embedding parameters, and KV cache, and it still finds looping wins, which makes it the most convincing evidence yet that depth reuse is real. Mixture-of-experts architectures are what make honest matching feasible. When looping costs extra FLOPs, the recipe narrows the hidden dimension; because MoE decouples total parameters from per-token compute, it then recovers the lost capacity by raising the expert count rather than giving it up; and KV cache parity is restored separately through head size and grouped-query-attention ratio, with every matched pair within four percent on FLOPs, one percent on parameters, and four percent on cache. item.title: UI-Venus-2 Technical Report
item.description: By Venus Team, Zhuohan Cai, Haoxing Chen (Ant Group) UI-Venus-2 Technical Report, by the Venus Team with Zhuohan Cai and Haoxing Chen, from Ant Group. This one lands under the standing rule for a reason: it is a technical report introducing a new general-purpose foundation GUI agent, and it is open-sourced, which is the part that matters most if you want to reproduce or build on it. The framing is practical, not speculative. GUI agents have moved fast on grounding and navigation benchmarks, but the authors argue that benchmark-oriented models do not transfer to dependable real-world use for three specific reasons. Environment coverage is too narrow to span multilingual mobile ecosystems, dynamic websites, and full desktop operating systems. Task construction is brittle, because generated queries often are not grounded in what an application can actually do. And the verification that supplies RL reward is unreliable, because a coarse verifier confuses partial progress with true completion, misses task-critical visual evidence, or exposes a reward a policy can exploit. The paper's design principle is that these three dimensions must be scaled jointly, not treated as independent knobs. The system is a unified closed-loop reasoning-and-action agent. Given a natural-language instruction, it observes rendered interface images, reasons about the task state, executes an action, and folds the resulting environmental feedback into the next decision. Two model sizes ship, a 9B and a 27B, both initialized from open-source Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-27B multimodal foundations. The action space is extended with desktop-specific actions so the same policy can operate on a phone, a browser, and an OS.

item.title: ZimaBlue: Evolving Generalizable World Action Models through Scalable Video Pre-training
item.description: By Xionghao Wu, Yijun Yang, Shiyang Zhou (Joy Future Academy) ZimaBlue is from Joy Future Academy, and the lead authors are Xionghao Wu, Yijun Yang, and Shiyang Zhou. It is a framework for building World Action Models, or WAMs, from large-scale video, and the central empirical claim is a scaling result: on real-robot zero-shot evaluation, going from target-robot data alone to over 120,000 hours of embodied video lifts task success from 36.1 percent to 77.8 percent. That is a big gap, and it is the whole argument in one sentence. The paper is a three-stage training framework, plus a deployment architecture, built to turn that gap into a practical system. The idea is to use each data source for its natural role. Stage one, video pre-training, learns causal visual dynamics from a huge corpus of first-person and robot egocentric video, with no action labels at all, starting from a generic text-to-video diffusion transformer called Wan2.2-TI2V-5B. Stage two, video-action mid-training, grounds those visual dynamics in actual robot control by introducing multi-embodiment robot trajectories with synchronized observations, proprioceptive states, language instructions, and actions, using a unified cross-embodiment action interface. Stage three, post-training, specializes the model to a single deployment embodiment and its action space, and this is where the fast branch enters. The unifying piece is the World Action Model itself, or WAM. Instead of a reactive policy that maps observation straight to action, a WAM jointly models how the visual world will evolve and what the robot should do within that evolution, with a single generative objective. The authors are explicit about why they do not just initialize from an off-the-shelf video generator. item.title: Hi-Q: Hierarchical Evidence-guided Query Refinement for Multi-Hop Question Answering
item.description: By Jueun Kim, Sungho Park, Wook-Shin Han (POSTECH) Hi-Q is from POSTECH, and the authors are Jueun Kim, Sungho Park, and Wook-Shin Han. It is a framework for multi-hop question answering that reframes the core difficulty as something specific: the granularity at which a question is expressed is usually different from the granularity at which the evidence for it is retrievable. The motivation is a single example they reuse throughout. When was the start of the battle of the birthplace of the performer of III? Answering that requires first identifying the performer of III, then that person's birthplace, and finally the start date of the battle at that location. One surface sentence, three dependent retrieval steps. The existing three families of methods each handle the mismatch in a way that misses when a query unit is already answerable. Single retrieval issues the coarse question once and hopes the top passages cover the whole chain. Graph RAG builds a fixed corpus-side structure before any query arrives, so the granularity is query-agnostic. Iterative retrieval adapts the query over time, but never tests whether the reformulation it just issued was actually supported by evidence, so an early wrong bridge propagates forward. Hi-Q's core idea is to make the decomposition decision evidence-conditioned rather than template-driven. It grows a query tree online. At each node, a resolution operator retrieves the top passages for the current query unit and has a retrieval-grounded reader try to answer from them. If the reader produces a real answer, the node is resolved and the branch terminates. If the reader returns nothing, the node is unresolved and becomes eligible for refinement. So the tree's topology is determined by corpus support signals, not by a fixed decomposition template or a pre-built graph.

item.title: DroneCATS: Evaluating Multimodal LLMs as Generalist Vision-Language-Action Agents for Drone Control
item.description: By Jaewoo Park, Minyoung Lee, Sukmin Seo (NAVER Cloud) DroneCATS, from Jaewoo Park, Minyoung Lee, and Sukmin Seo, among the NAVER Cloud drone AI team. This is a benchmark and a reference agent for putting a multimodal large language model directly inside a drone's control loop. The question is what happens when you stop engineering responsibility out of the model. Recent systems that fly drones with an MLLM almost all subtract: TypeFly keeps the model as a planner over detections, See Point Fly reduces control to pointing at a pixel, Fly0 confines the model to grounding and hands trajectory generation to a separate planner, and OnFly adds a verifier that corrects the model before its output reaches the actuators. Each takes something away and then reports that it works. But that workflow varies the system and holds the model fixed, so it can answer how much the model can do once you remove parts of the job, not which parts of embodied drone control actually depend on the model. DroneCATS asks the converse. It holds the agent fixed and varies the model, so the backbone is the independent variable. The agent is deliberately minimal. It is a model-agnostic wrapper in which the entire action space is declared in natural language in the prompt, with no fine-tuning, no action head, and no function-calling schema. The model is a swappable component, and swapping it changes nothing else around it. It works at a high level on four primitives. The first is go, which carries a pixel and a depth estimate, and a rule-based controller back-projects that pair into a three-dimensional displacement and hands it to the flight stack as a velocity setpoint. The model never emits a velocity or an attitude. The second is rotate, an in-place yaw, which is the only way to look for a target that is out of frame. item.title: Safin-1: Safety from Within through Memory-Native State Evolution
item.description: By Ming Zhang, Kaisen Yang, Shu Yu (Shanghai AI Laboratory) Safin-1, from the Safin team at Shanghai AI Laboratory, with Ming Zhang, Kaisen Yang, and Shu Yu among the contributors. This is an architecture paper that asks whether safety can live inside a model's own computation rather than being bolted on as an external constraint. The starting point is a distinction most alignment work quietly blurs. A language model retains context in one substrate, a token-level cache or a recurrent state, but it encodes reusable behaviors like safety in a different one, model updates, adapters, or learned prefixes imposed at inference time. The paper's claim is that these should be the same substrate. It calls the principle Safety from Within: safety-relevant capabilities should be represented and invoked through the model's native computation, not through post-hoc alignment that depends on external safeguards. The mechanism is a new architecture called MARCH, Memory-Anchor Routing across Context History, which turns the transient trajectory of a recurrent model into a growing bank of addressable states that the model can selectively read back. The architecture solves a specific failure of recurrent models. Self-attention keeps fine-grained access to every prior token but pays a quadratic training cost and a key-value cache that grows with sequence length. Recurrent and linear-attention models compress the prefix into a fixed-size state for constant-memory decoding, but they expose only the latest state for reading, so once an earlier association is attenuated or overwritten, it is gone. MARCH fixes that by periodically checkpointing the evolving recurrent state. At boundaries placed every 512 tokens, the model snapshots its cumulative state into a state anchor and pairs it with a compact routing key. item.title: Does On-Policy Distillation Really Distill? From Noisy Teacher to Self-Improvement
item.description: By Yi Ding, Ruqi Zhang (Purdue University) Does On-Policy Distillation Really Distill? From Noisy Teacher to Self-Improvement, by Yi Ding and Ruqi Zhang, from the Department of Computer Science at Purdue University. The short version of a long argument: on-policy distillation, one of the most popular token-level post-training recipes of the last year, is not actually distilling. The students get better, but the gains come from suppressing the model's own low-probability tokens, an operation that needs no teacher at all. The authors demonstrate this with controlled ablations, then turn the diagnosis into OPSA, a supervision-free training rule that beats on-policy distillation by 16.77 points on AIME24. To set up the problem: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, like GRPO and DAPO, samples a group of responses per question and normalizes the verifiable rewards within the group to get advantages. The weakness is sparsity. When several responses in a group get the same correctness outcome, their normalized advantages vanish and the learning signal dies. On-policy distillation fixes that with dense supervision: a stronger teacher scores every token of the student's own rollouts, and the per-token advantage is the log-ratio of the teacher's probability over the student's, a reverse KL estimator. The catch is practical: you need shared vocabularies and white-box access to teacher logits. On-policy self-distillation keeps the paradigm but swaps in a hinted version of the policy itself as teacher. The authors argue all of these share the same fatal assumption: that a teacher scoring prefixes it would never generate itself is still giving meaningful supervision.

item.title: PaperGym: Rubric-Centered Evolution for Research-Plan Generation
item.description: By Yuhan Wang, Zhengxi Lu, Yuchen Yan (Zhejiang University) PaperGym: Rubric-Centered Evolution for Research-Plan Generation, by Yuhan Wang, Zhengxi Lu, and Yuchen Yan, from Zhejiang University. The problem it targets: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has no home for research planning, because a research plan has no checkable answer. Math and code generation work with RLVR because every problem ships with an automatic checker. A research plan does not. You cannot diff a proposed experimental design against a golden file, and expert review does not scale to training. So how do you train a model to write good research plans? The scientific literature already contains the raw material at scale: millions of papers, each posing a realistic problem and developing a solution. PaperGym is a framework that converts each paper into a complete training environment, with a question, a reference answer, and a grading rubric, and then trains on it in two stages. The authors release the pipeline, a corpus of 20,000 instances called PaperGym-20k, and two held-out benchmarks. The data construction is the first contribution, and it targets a real flaw in prior rubric-based datasets. Existing pipelines pull the question and the grading criteria from the same part of a paper, so the criteria often restate the question. The authors measured this: in existing datasets, 11.90 to 34.10 percent of criteria can be inferred from the question alone. That means a model can raise its reward by paraphrasing the question back at the judge. PaperGym instead exploits paper structure. It decomposes each paper into four stages, Research Goal, Background, Research Method, and Experimental Design, using a map-reduce extraction with Qwen3-235B-A22B. The question is synthesized only from the Research Goal and Background; the reference answer is derived only from the Research Method and Experim

item.title: CogEvol: Towards Efficient and Reliable Learning Environment Generation
item.description: By Shangqing Tu, Daniel Zhang-Li, Yucheng Wang (CogEvol Inc.; Tsinghua University) CogEvol: Towards Efficient and Reliable Learning Environment Generation, by the CogEvol Team, from CogEvol Inc. and Tsinghua University, with first authors Shangqing Tu, Daniel Zhang-Li, and Yucheng Wang. This is a new foundation-model family, and that matters for this show. CogEvol is a pair of models, a 4B and a 27B, trained specifically for one narrow job: Learning Environment Generation. Given a course brief, it produces a finished learning artifact in a single pass, either structured-JSON slides or a self-contained interactive HTML page. The claim is efficiency and reliability: across 220,000 production requests, a slide completes in a median of 17 seconds and an interactive page in 59, replacing the minutes-long multi-turn agent scaffolding that was the incumbent approach. The 4B is released openly under Apache 2.0; the 27B has served live production traffic in collaboration with the OpenMAIC team since August 2026. I will be precise about one thing up front. CogEvol is built entirely through post-training on top of public base models. The 27B starts from Qwen3.8-27B, a hybrid architecture interleaving 48 gated-delta-net linear-attention layers with 16 full-attention layers and a multi-token-prediction head; the 4B starts from the dense Qwen3.5-4B. The authors contribute everything above the base: the data pipelines, hybrid reward and RL recipes, evaluation suites, and serving infrastructure. So this is a capability release, not a new pre-trained base, and I am flagging it as a foundation-model technical report in the sense the standing rule intends, a new named family of production models for a specific task, not because they trained a transformer from scratch.

item.title: Normalized Low-Rank Adaptation
item.description: By Jiale Kang, Ziyin Yue, Zheng Zhan (Yuanshi Intelligence; Microsoft Research; CUHK) Normalized Low-Rank Adaptation, by Jiale Kang, Ziyin Yue, and Zheng Zhan, from Yuanshi Intelligence, Microsoft Research, and the Chinese University of Hong Kong. The one-line version: normalizing LoRA's down-projection matrix, either continuously or just at initialization, consistently speeds up convergence and improves accuracy across pretraining, finetuning, and reinforcement learning, with no extra parameters or inference cost. LoRA is the default tool for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and the reasons are practical: you train a tiny low-rank pair of matrices instead of the full weights, and the update can be merged back into the base model at deployment. But the training dynamics of that low-rank pair have never really been interrogated. The observation this paper builds on is asymmetric: because LoRA initializes the up-projection to zero, the very first gradients flow almost entirely through the down-projection. Whatever the scale structure of that down-projection is at step zero largely dictates the early trajectory of the whole adapter, and that structure is currently left to random initialization. The fix is a one-line constraint. For a down-projection A with rank dimension r, NoRA normalizes each column of A to unit norm along the rank direction, so every input coordinate is projected through a unit-length latent direction. The key design choice is that this normalization depends on the LoRA parameters, not on the input. That keeps the update linear in the input, which means the normalized adapter can still be absorbed into the pretrained weight matrix after training. You keep the mergeability that makes LoRA deployable, and you only pay a per-step normalization during training.

item.title: SHAPE of Chain-of-Thought in Math Reasoning
item.description: By Jonghyun Song, Sangjun Song, Minjae Oh (Seoul National University) SHAPE of Chain-of-Thought in Math Reasoning, by Jonghyun Song, Sangjun Song, and Minjae Oh, from the Graduate School of Data Science and the Department of Mathematics Education at Seoul National University. The premise: stop treating a math chain-of-thought as a bag of tokens and start reading it the way a mathematics educator would, tracking which interpretation of the problem the model is working in and which concrete mathematical moves it makes. The framework, called SHAPE, borrows two objects from decades of mathematical problem-solving research. The first is a semantic space, the evolving interpretation under which the model is solving a problem, algebraic, geometric, numerical, and so on. A single correct solution can move between several of these; the model might set up an equation, abandon it to try concrete numbers, then come back to the algebra. The second is a heuristic, the visible mathematical action taken inside a space: simplifying the problem, working backward, introducing an auxiliary object, making cases. These come from Pólya, Schoenfeld, and the think-aloud protocol tradition in mathematics education, where a human solver's verbalizations have been coded into exactly this kind of space-and-move structure for decades. The pipeline is an annotator, they use Grok-4.1-Fast for the labeling, that reads a CoT trace content unit by content unit, tags the heuristic of each unit, and tracks the semantic-space state as it changes, maintaining a memory buffer so it knows when the model is returning to a space it already visited versus opening a new one.

item.title: Scaling Large Reasoning Models beyond Human Supervision: A Path toward Superintelligence
item.description: By Zhiqin Yang, Jingwen Fu, Yuhan Liu (HKUST; Zhongguancun Academy; Xi'an Jiaotong University) Scaling Large Reasoning Models beyond Human Supervision, by Zhiqin Yang, Jingwen Fu, and Yuhan Liu, from HKUST, the Zhongguancun Academy, and Xi'an Jiaotong University, with a large corresponding-author team spanning a dozen institutions. The question it organizes around: as large reasoning models keep improving, human supervision is gradually receding from the learning loop, so how does a model keep getting better once the person who wrote the answer, or the rubric, or the environment, is no longer in the room? This is a survey and a position paper, not a new method, and I want to be clear about that from the start. Its value is as a map. It builds a taxonomy that the field has been using inconsistently, and it maintains a continuously updated GitHub repository that tracks the latest systems as they appear. The central organizing device is a five-level ladder, L0 through L4, that classifies where the supervision in a training loop is coming from, and which parts of the loop are still under human control. The ladder is worth stating in full because it is the paper's main contribution. L0 is per-instance human supervision: every training example is paired with a human-provided answer, preference, or judgment that is its target. That is classic supervised learning and the human-in-the-loop reward modeling of early RLHF. L1 is human-grounded evaluation: the human criteria are encoded once into a reusable reward model, rubric, or language-model judge, so the same standard can be applied across many trajectories without a person looking at each one. item.title: DART-SD: Diamond-topology Aware Retrieval and Tuning for Self-Distillation of Multi-Turn Tool-Calling Agents
item.description: By Hangrui Xu, Jiarui Wang, Yang Yang (ByteDance; University of Science and Technology of China) DART-SD: Diamond-topology Aware Retrieval and Tuning for Self-Distillation of Multi-Turn Tool-Calling Agents, by Hangrui Xu, Jiarui Wang, and Yang Yang of ByteDance, with further authors and Yan Song of the University of Science and Technology of China. The paper attacks a specific, expensive failure in agent training: when a compact student imitates a frontier teacher on multi-turn tool-calling tasks, the standard recipes, full-trajectory supervised fine-tuning and grouped reinforcement learning, both flatten what is actually a graph into a line, and that flattening has a measurable cost. The structural claim first. For tasks with order-independent sub-goals, say fetch three independent facts before writing the answer, many action orders are equally valid, and distinct trajectories routinely diverge and then reconverge at the same intermediate state, because what matters is the information acquired, not the tool syntax that acquired it. The optimal solution space is a combinatorial diamond lattice. Full-trajectory SFT forces every valid ordering to compete against one canonical ordering, so it overwrites valid exploration; the authors call this topological collapse. Grouped reinforcement learning has the mirror-image failure: a terminal reward spread across all tokens penalizes perfectly fine intermediate tool calls inside failed trajectories, credit misassignment. Hindsight methods that relabel failed trajectories still treat the interaction as a linear sequence and cannot tell fatal errors from harmless detours.

item.title: J-ZERO: Unified Challenger-Solver-Judge Co-Evolution from Zero Data
item.description: By Gyouk Chu, Myeongho Jeon, Eunho Yang (KAIST) J-ZERO: Unified Challenger-Solver-Judge Co-Evolution from Zero Data, by Gyouk Chu, Myeongho Jeon, and Eunho Yang of KAIST. Zero-data self-play is now a real thing: one model spawns a Challenger that invents tasks and a Solver that learns to answer them, with no external data. It works well where answers can be checked, code execution or majority voting. It stalls everywhere else, because in open-ended domains the learning signal is a reward model, and a frozen judge can only push the solver toward preferences the judge has already internalized. Once the solver saturates the distinctions the judge can make, training produces nothing. The prior fix, G-Zero, kept the judge frozen and worked around it. This paper's move is more direct: let the judge co-evolve inside the loop, and solve the circularity problem, if every signal comes from the same system, what new preference information ever enters, by constructing preference labels from structural asymmetries that hold by construction, independent of any judge scores. The loop has three roles and three phases per iteration. The Challenger generates tasks; its reward is one minus the mean judge score of the solver's attempts on the task, minus a repetition penalty computed by clustering near-duplicate tasks with pairwise BLEU distance, with a format check requiring a well-formed question tag; malformed generations get a negative reward. It is trained with grouped policy optimization to minimize that composite reward, adversarial but deliberately not zero-sum, since the challenger also has diversity and validity constraints. item.title: Fast Weight Attention for Continual Learning
item.description: By Yifan Zhang, Steve Ta, Jasper Zhang (ByteDance Seed; Princeton University; Tsinghua University; UCLA; Hyperbolic Labs) Fast Weight Attention for Continual Learning, by Yifan Zhang of ByteDance Seed and Princeton University, Steve Ta and Jasper Zhang, with further authors from ByteDance Seed, Princeton, Tsinghua, UCLA, and Hyperbolic Labs, including Andrew Chi-Chih Yao among the corresponding authors. The framing is worth pausing on, because it reframes an architecture debate as a learning problem. Standard attention externalizes memory as a growing key-value cache: nothing is ever compressed, nothing is ever forgotten, and quadratic cost follows. State-space models and fast-weight architectures instead compress the whole context into a fixed-size recurrent state, which means the state update is literally an online learning rule, a little gradient step executed every token, inside the forward pass. Seen that way, the real design question for these architectures is not what shape the state has but what objective that internal learning rule is actually optimizing, and when it gets to see its training pairs. That question has been implicit in every linear-attention and Delta-network paper so far; this one makes it explicit and finds that the field has been using the wrong pairing. The central observation is a one-position misalignment. Under read-after-write autoregressive semantics, when the model is predicting token t, the state it reads was last written at t minus one; the value that becomes available at step t should therefore be bound to the prefix feature that was available when it was predicted, the key from the previous position, not the key from the current one. Most prior recurrences bind the same-step pair, current key with current value. item.title: Blind Men and the Elephant: Probing the Epistemic Myopia of LLMs under Long-Tail Divergent Knowledge

The benchmark asks a question that standard factual QA cannot ask: not whether a model knows a rare fact, but whether it knows all the credible versions of that fact that its training data contained. The parable in the title is the failure mode: each blind man touches one part of the elephant and generalizes; a model that read one account of a disputed birth date and only ever reproduces that account has the same pathology, and because conventional QA scores a single canonical answer, the pathology is invisible. The evaluation is fully closed-book: no source documents, no retrieval, no tools, just the question, so whatever the model answers comes from parametric memory alone, which is what makes the measurement about what training actually retained rather than about reasoning over evidence. The construction pipeline is the reusable contribution. It starts from the filtered remainder of a web corpus, the documents a standard quality classifier, the DCLM fastText filter, throws away, because low-exposure documents are where disagreements survive unharmonized and where pretraining upsampling is least likely to have distorted exposure. Documents become nodes in a graph; support edges connect documents about the same fact, conflict edges connect documents reporting incompatible accounts of the same subject-attribute pair. item.title: StepGuard: Learning Step-Level Guardrails with Scalable Supervision and Safety-Utility Balancing
item.description: By Zhijie Zheng, Yu Li, Chen Qian (Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory; Beihang University; Fudan University; Renmin University of China; KAUST) StepGuard: Learning Step-Level Guardrails with Scalable Supervision and Safety-Utility Balancing, by Zhijie Zheng and Yu Li of the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory with Beihang University, Chen Qian with Renmin University of China, and colleagues at Fudan University and KAUST. The premise: agents invoke tools, and tool invocation is where prompt injections turn into real damage, files modified, messages sent, secrets disclosed. Most guardrails audit whole trajectories after the fact. This paper builds a four-billion-parameter guard that checks each candidate tool call before it executes, and attacks the two things that make such guards hard to train: there is almost no real-world data on unsafe executions to learn from, and every guard in the wild has a defense bias, either blocking too many benign actions or missing too many risky ones. The data engine, StepGen, is the first contribution. Real unsafe executions are too rare to supervise at scale, so it synthesizes them in a controlled way that isolates the actual decision point. For each scenario it samples a risk source, a failure mode, and a harm type, then has a planner compile a task into a structured execution plan with a designated unsafe anchor step. The plan is rolled out through an environment simulator into an unsafe base trajectory; for response-borne risks like indirect prompt injection, the simulator plants the perturbation in the environment context available at exactly the anchor step, so the anchor is the first unsafe decision, not an inherited one. item.description: By Shudong Liu, Dongyang Chen, Enci Zhang (Peking University; Tsinghua University; SenseTime Research) Paint What You See: Benchmarking Dexterous Visual Tool Use in Multimodal Agents, by Shudong Liu of Peking University and SenseTime Research, Dongyang Chen of Tsinghua University and SenseTime, and Enci Zhang of Peking University, with further authors from SenseTime. The capability being tested is one those benchmarks cannot see: fine-grained, closed-loop, parameterized visual action. The agent looks at a reference image and a canvas, emits a brush stroke as thirteen continuous parameters, a quadratic Bezier path with start, control, and end points, per-endpoint radius and opacity, and a shared color, the renderer applies it, and the updated canvas comes back as feedback. Every parameter directly shapes the result; nothing absorbs imprecision. The authors call it dexterous visual tool use, by analogy with robot manipulation, and contrast it with everything current benchmarks measure: web and GUI agents succeed inside generous tolerance regions, and visual editing agents delegate execution to external generative models. Here there is no tolerant region and no delegating. The benchmark, EASEL, centers on reference-guided reconstruction: one hundred ten samples across four difficulty tiers, from programmatic shapes at sixty-four by sixty-four with a thirty-two-step budget up to natural images at one hundred twenty-eight with one hundred twenty-eight steps, plus five semantic tasks, two outline-annotation tasks scored by Dice coefficient, a handwriting task, and two mazes scored by path progress, all told up to eleven thousand three hundred ninety-two interactions for a full evaluation. item.title: PonderPounce: A Pretrained MLLM as an Episode Context Engine for Robot Control
item.description: By Suhwan Choi, Jaeyoon Jung, Sungkyung Kim (MAUM.AI; Seoul National University) PonderPounce: A Pretrained MLLM as an Episode Context Engine for Robot Control, by Suhwan Choi and Jaeyoon Jung of MAUM.AI, with Sungkyung Kim, Yunsung Lee, and Youngjae Yu splitting time between MAUM.AI and Seoul National University. Robot policies that must act on things they saw earlier, an object that is now occluded, an event that already happened, a demonstration of what to do, have no good place to put that memory. Vision-language-action models inherit rich pretrained representations but do not use their contextual capacity as episode memory; purpose-built memory systems instead add frame samplers, storage banks, retrieval paths, or compressors, each an architecture-specific mechanism to design and tune. This paper tries the simplest possible answer to the question of where episode memory should live: in the native causal context of a pretrained multimodal language model, read out to the controller through one continuous token. The architecture is a two-system split with dual-process naming. Ponder, System Two, is a nine-B multimodal model, initialized from Qwen3.5-nine B, that maintains an append-only context holding the instruction, optional demonstration videos, every observation so far, its own internally generated subgoal text and demonstration reasoning, and its previous cognition carriers. The final hidden states of the carrier positions form the cognition, passed downstream. item.description: By Pengfei Zhou, Hexin Wang, Zhengfeiyang Zhang (National University of Singapore; HPC-AI Lab; InfRec, Cardinal AI Lab; University of California, Berkeley; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology) Agentic Game Development as a Verifiable Trajectory Data Engine for Scaling World Models, by Pengfei Zhou of the National University of Singapore, Hexin Wang and Zhengfeiyang Zhang of Cardinal AI Lab, with further authors from the University of California, Berkeley, and the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. The paper makes an argument before it runs a single experiment, and the argument is worth taking seriously: world models are not stuck because of missing video, they are stuck because there is no cheap way to check whether a generated world is correct. Code agents escaped this problem because a compiler grades every patch. Spatial generation has no compiler, only fuzzy proxies like CLIP similarity, so the authors propose to use game development itself as the reward engine, and to train an agent that builds worlds inside a real game workflow so the workflow becomes the dataset. The framing is a re-reading of the Bitter Lesson. The usual summary says general methods that scale with compute beat hand-designed priors. This paper says that reading is incomplete for domains like code, games, and math, because in those domains scalable learning is paired with an evaluator that defines success: program execution, game rules, numerical checkers. The lesson is that the efficient gain comes from the feedback channel, not from the architecture. Once a scalable reward mechanism exists, compute can search for candidates that satisfy it. When it does not exist, scaling still improves imitation and perceptual plausibility, but nothing enforces correctness. item.title: UrbanGround: From Local Perception to Spatial Agency in a Real-Scale City
item.description: By Tianjie Ju, Zheng Wu, Yueqing Sun (Shanghai Jiao Tong University; National University of Singapore; Meituan; The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Shanghai University; University of Oxford) UrbanGround: From Local Perception to Spatial Agency in a Real-Scale City, by Tianjie Ju of Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Zheng Wu of Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Meituan, and Yueqing Sun of Meituan, with further authors from the National University of Singapore, the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shanghai University, and the University of Oxford. The question is simple to state and hard to test: a multimodal model can describe a street view, but can it keep using that understanding after it starts walking? Turn a corner and the landmark that justified your last decision disappears, while its location still matters. The authors built a physically constrained replica of the whole of Hong Kong to find out, and the answer is that current agents hold up for one look and fall apart over a route. First, the environment, because that is the actual artifact. The team took two public datasets from the Lands Department of the Hong Kong government: a three-D visualisation map, a tile-based textured mesh reconstructed from oblique aerial imagery covering the full territory, and a three-D pedestrian network of georeferenced walkable segments. Both are streamed into Unity in a shared geographic frame, tiles load according to the viewing scale, and the tile geometry serves double duty as rendered surface and collision geometry, so buildings and elevation changes physically constrain the agent. item.title: Self-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Flow Matching Models without Teacher
item.description: By Shiyi Zhang, Mushui Liu, Yunze Tong (Tsinghua University; Zhejiang University; Alibaba Group) Self-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Flow Matching Models without Teacher, by Shiyi Zhang of Tsinghua University and Alibaba Group, Mushui Liu of Zhejiang University and Alibaba Group, and Yunze Tong of Zhejiang University, with further authors from Alibaba Group. The paper targets an expensive habit in generative-model alignment: every time you want to steer a flow-matching image model toward a new objective, the on-policy distillation approach says train a specialized teacher first, then distill from it. Three objectives, three teachers, weeks of GPU time before the student learns anything. Self-OPD removes the teacher entirely and shows the student can generate its own step-wise supervision by exploring around its own trajectory, and the resulting model beats teacher-based distillation on the paper's mixed-objective benchmark. The two prior paradigms frame the problem. Reinforcement-learning approaches like Flow-GRPO treat denoising as a sequential decision process, but the reward arrives only at the end of the full denoising trajectory, so credit must be assigned backward through many steps with high-variance gradients, and mixing several reward models makes multi-objective training fragile because different rewards favor different visual properties. On-policy distillation gives dense, per-step supervision by regressing the student's velocity field toward a pretrained teacher's prediction at every denoising step, which is stable and sample-efficient, but each new objective needs its own teacher, the student is capped by that teacher's quality and bias, and merging multiple teachers at the velocity-field level creates conflicting update directions. Self-OPD keeps the dense per-step structure and replaces the teacher with the student's own local exploration.

item.title: TTPO: Test-Time Policy Optimization
item.description: By Aozhe Wang, Zhengxi Lu, Jianze Wang (Zhejiang University; Alibaba Group) TTPO: Test-Time Policy Optimization, by Aozhe Wang of Zhejiang University and Alibaba Group, Zhengxi Lu of Zhejiang University, and Jianze Wang of Alibaba Group, with further authors from both institutions. The setting is test-time training: a model improves on the very problems it is about to be evaluated on, with no answer key, because labels never arrive. Every strong post-training recipe we have, reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards and on-policy self-distillation, assumes an oracle that grades outputs or hands the teacher the right answer. TTPO's contribution is an asymmetric objective that survives a majority-vote pseudo-label being wrong, which on competition math it usually is, and the empirical claim is that this label-free recipe matches the label-supervised version. The problem structure first. Sample a group of rollouts per problem, cluster the final answers by mathematical equivalence, and take the largest cluster as the pseudo-label. On AIME 2026 with the Qwen3 one point seven B base model, that pseudo-label is wrong for about eighty-five percent of prompts. The prior approaches all break on this. TTRL uses the pseudo-label as a reward, so a wrong majority reinforces its own error once per trajectory. The dangerous variant is dense supervision: condition the same model on the pseudo-answer to form a teacher, and distill the student toward it. A corrupted reward misleads once per trajectory; a corrupted teacher misleads at every token.

item.title: What Makes Good Agentic Data? An ACE Lens on Data Generation for LLM Agents
item.description: By Xingshan Zeng, Zishan Xu, Boju Zhang (Huawei Technologies; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Northwestern University; Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen; Shenzhen Loop Area Institute) What Makes Good Agentic Data? An ACE Lens on Data Generation for LLM Agents, by Xingshan Zeng of Huawei Technologies, Zishan Xu and Boju Zhang of Shanghai Jiao Tong University, with further authors from Northwestern University, Harbin Institute of Technology in Shenzhen, and the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute. This is a survey, not a system paper, but it earns its forty minutes of your attention by doing the two things a good survey should: it replaces a pile of domain-specific vocabulary with one abstraction that actually holds across domains, and it states the field's implicit objective function out loud. If you are building an agent data pipeline this quarter, this is the map. The core object. Agentic data is not instruction-response pairs. The paper factorizes every agentic training example as four components: E, the environment specification, from bare tool schemas up to fully executable simulators with state, dynamics, policies, and observation interfaces; q, the task signal, which may be an explicit instruction, a hidden user intent, or something progressively revealed across turns; tau, the interaction realization, the actual trajectory of actions and observations; and v, an optional verifier, which can be a schema checker, executable test, state predicate, proof assistant, or model judge. The decomposition is conceptual rather than a serialization requirement, but it makes the real content of the field visible: pipelines generate not just conversations but tool ecosystems, executable environments, stateful tasks, and verification procedures, and the hard engineering is keeping those four factors consistent with each other. item.title: Training Agents to Evolve with Their Harness: TaoLive Digital Avatar Agent Technical Report
item.description: By TaoLive AIGC LLM Team, Yuhan Sun, Wenhao Lin (Alibaba Group) Training Agents to Evolve with Their Harness: TaoLive Digital Avatar Agent Technical Report, by the TaoLive AIGC LLM team at Alibaba, with Yuhan Sun and Wenhao Lin among the listed authors. The setting is live-stream e-commerce: an AI avatar answers product questions and runs marketing playbooks on air, where every reply is public, the latency budget is seconds, and the business rules change weekly. The engineering dilemma is real and worth stating plainly. Big models adapt to new rules zero-shot but are too slow; in their tests a frontier model's median end-to-end latency exceeded eleven seconds. Compact models meet the latency target but, trained on one fixed configuration, they memorize skill names, tool names, and prompt templates, and then fail exactly when the harness they memorized changes. Fixed-harness supervised fine-tuning costs seven point seven points on IFEval, a general instruction-following benchmark, which is the measurable signature of that overfitting. Their production answer is an evolvable harness with four independently versioned modules: Skills, which are reply rules and strategies; Hooks, which are validation checkpoints that can force retries; a system prompt pipeline; and a tool registry wired to commerce services. Behavior changes ship as harness edits, not retraining. A human-in-the-loop process they call harness evolution diagnoses failures, proposes edits, and evaluates: on a development set of four hundred eighty-two cases annotated by three people, the first evolution round lifted accuracy from eighty-two point four to ninety-two point one but dropped effectiveness to eighty-four point two, the second round reached ninety-two point six and ninety-two point eight and was selected as the engineering stopping point, and further long-tail rules regressed one or both dimensions.

item.title: VoiceMem: Streaming Dual-Brain Memory for Real-Time Interaction
item.description: By Zhifei Xie, Jiaqi Lang, Ze An (Nanyang Technological University; National University of Singapore; Tsinghua University; Chinese University of Hong Kong; Open Interaction Lab) VoiceMem: Streaming Dual-Brain Memory for Real-Time Interaction, by Zhifei Xie of Nanyang Technological University, Jiaqi Lang and Ze An of the National University of Singapore, with further authors from Tsinghua University, the Chinese University of Hong Kong, and the Open Interaction Lab. The paper opens with a quote from Plato about memory being the mother of wisdom, which is a bold choice for a systems paper, but the substance underneath is real: duplex speech models — systems built to talk with you, interrupt you, and overlap your turns — have no usable long-term memory, because their entire retrieval budget is half a second. Classic text memory engines retrieve the top one hundred memories from a vector store in two to three seconds; a voice agent must detect that the user stopped talking, decide what to recall, and start speaking within roughly five hundred milliseconds of voice-activity-pause detection. VoiceMem's answer is an architecture that retrieves useful context in about one hundred thirty-four milliseconds, plus a training recipe that manufactures the conversation data no public corpus provides. The layout is two brains over one index, and the separation is worth copying even if you never build a voice product. The left brain handles information: facts, preferences, events — anything answerable by lookup. The right brain handles persona and affect: stable user traits on independent nodes, plus cross-entity nodes binding attitudes to specific entities, so the system can distinguish "this person likes hiking" from "this person has been complaining about their knee since May." item.title: FrontierChallenge: Evaluating Scientific Workflow Completion
item.description: By Apodex Team (Apodex) FrontierChallenge: Evaluating Scientific Workflow Completion, by the Apodex Team — a benchmark paper with an unusually honest byline: no individual author list at all, just a team name, a leaderboard site, an open evaluation harness on GitHub, and a dataset release. The premise: frontier labs publish agentic coding results on software benchmarks where tests can be run in seconds, but real scientific work is not a pull request. A computational chemistry task means installing ORCA or LAMMPS, running simulations that take hours, producing tables, figures, and code that all have to agree with each other — and nobody grades whether the bundle hangs together. FrontierChallenge tries to grade exactly that, and its verdict on twelve frontier models across three agent scaffolds is blunt: the best configuration completes twenty out of ninety-seven tasks, roughly one in five, and more than three quarters of failing runs still claimed they had succeeded. The measurement design matters as much as the numbers, so it is worth walking through how you score a scientific artifact fairly. The authors curated three hundred end-to-end workflows from six computational domains and released ninety-seven of them — seventy-four rated hard, twenty-three medium — keeping two hundred three internal for held-out testing. The domain spread is deliberate: twenty quantum chemistry tasks, twenty-two materials characterization, twenty-three analytical chemistry, sixteen molecular dynamics, ten life science, six electrochemistry and environment, spanning twenty-one workflow families. Every task ships fixed inputs, a required toolchain — ORCA, CP2K, LAMMPS, AmberTools, PLUMED at various points — and a task-specific executable grader that checks the whole deliverable bundle: reports, tables, figures, code, and simulation products must be mutually consistent. item.title: WarpSAC: Rethinking Off-Policy Stabilizers for Massively Parallel Reinforcement Learning
item.description: By Zihao Wu, Hongyao Tang, Yi Ma (Tianjin University; Shanxi University; Imperial College London) WarpSAC: Rethinking Off-Policy Stabilizers for Massively Parallel Reinforcement Learning, by Zihao Wu of Tianjin University, Hongyao Tang of Shanxi University, Yi Ma of Imperial College London, and colleagues including Jianye Hao. The title is a Star Trek reference — a footnote dutifully credits the warp drive to the nineteen seventy-nine motion picture — but the paper underneath is one of the cleaner controlled studies RL has produced this year. Its thesis lands like heresy against a decade of received wisdom: the stabilization tricks that every off-policy algorithm ships by default — replay weighting, clipped double critics, parameter normalization — were designed for a world of scarce data, and in the world of massively parallel GPU simulation where thousands of environments generate experience faster than the learner can consume it, those same tricks measurably hold you back. Sometimes the right move is to delete your stabilizers. The framing is what makes this more than an ablation dump. The authors refuse to ask whether each component is good or bad; they ask when its benefits outweigh its restrictions. Their target backbone is FlashSAC, a recent soft actor-critic variant, and they vary exactly three axes, each representing one classical stabilizer. First, replay weighting: standard practice reweights uniform sampling by priorities; they replace it with Sample Weight Decay, which biases weights toward fresh samples by decaying them with age while a floor keeps old data from vanishing entirely — turn the decay horizon to zero and you recover plain uniform replay. item.title: JIT-Agent: Model-as-a-Harness — Training a Meta-Agent to Compile Agent Harnesses On the Fly
item.description: By Guibin Zhang, Leo Lu, Fangzhou Xie (LV-NUS Lab, National University of Singapore) JIT-Agent, from Guibin Zhang, Leo Lu, Fangzhou Xie, and colleagues at the LV-NUS Lab in Singapore — a paper whose one-line pitch is an equation: agent capability equals model times harness, so stop hand-designing harnesses and train a model to write them. The authors observe that harness engineering has become the field's most labor-intensive craft: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and yes — Hermes, which their related-work table lists among thirteen representative scaffolds they re-implemented as seed data — are all fixed, ahead-of-time artifacts, tuned once and shipped to every task. The alternative this paper builds is called Model-as-a-Harness: take an off-the-shelf agentic LLM and train a meta-agent that synthesizes a task-specific, executable harness at deployment time, compiled fresh per task like just-in-time code. Hence the name. The formalism earns its keep. A harness is defined as a composable four-tuple: memory module, planning structure, action space, and capability orchestration, all under a fixed protocol. Classic ReAct becomes full-context memory, no planner, direct actions, monolithic orchestration. Codex-style coding agents become compacted memory plus a todo-list planner. Recursive multi-agent frameworks become subproblem memory, decomposition planning, recursive actions, routing orchestration. Thirteen real scaffolds are factorized into coordinates in this design space and serve as the seed bank. The meta-agent's job is to navigate that space: given a task description, generate a harness instance — actual executable code for memory, planning, tool dispatch — rather than pick one off the shelf. item.title: D³-MOPD: Dynamic Mixture Scheduling for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
item.description: By AllSpark Team (AllSpark Team) D-cubed MOPD, full title Dynamic Data-wise Mixture Scheduling for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation, comes from the AllSpark Team. The problem it attacks will be familiar to anyone who has trained a model against multiple objectives: when you distill from several specialist teachers at once — one for mathematics, one for code, one for instruction following, one for tool use — you must decide how to split your training batch among them. Standard practice fixes that mixture once at the start, in proportion to dataset sizes or gut feel, and holds it constant for the entire run. The paper's central observation is that domains converge at wildly different speeds, so any fixed mixture is wrong for almost the whole run: by mid-training some domains have already plateaued and are soaking up compute producing no progress, while others still need everything they can get. First, the base recipe their scheduler plugs into, because it is elegant enough on its own. On-policy distillation has the student generate its own rollouts; each domain teacher then prefills those same rollouts, scoring what the student actually produced rather than what a reference would have said; the student minimizes per-token reverse KL divergence to the teacher along that trajectory. Run four domain-specialist teachers this way simultaneously and one unified student model inherits all four skills without ever serving the specialists at inference time. item.title: Agent-G²: Guidance as a Per-Task Distribution for Sparse-Reward Agent RL
item.description: By Zixuan Wang, Yanrui Miao, Yongliang Shen (Zhejiang University; Baidu) Agent-G-squared: Guidance as a Gaussian distribution per task — from Zixuan Wang and Yanrui Miao of Zhejiang University working with Baidu, corresponding author Yongliang Shen. The problem is the classic wall in agent reinforcement learning: long-horizon tasks like operating a simulated household or completing a shopping order give almost no reward until suddenly all of it at the end, so during early training the policy wanders in a reward desert where gradient estimates are pure noise. Hint-based methods climb that wall by replaying a prefix of an expert trajectory — hand the agent the first portion of a known-good solution, let it explore onward from there, so its rollouts land near success and rewards finally flow. But this creates a new knob with real teeth: guidance depth, how much prefix to keep before handing control back. Keep too little and successes remain vanishingly rare; keep too much and every rollout succeeds, rewards saturate, and advantage estimation inside group-relative optimization loses all contrast — nothing to learn from either direction. The knob punishes both ends asymmetrically but reliably, which is why nobody wants to tune it by hand. Prior approaches treat that knob two ways, and the paper's diagnostic dismantles both. Schedule families — linear decay, cosine decay, step schedules, accuracy-triggered adjustments — assign one depth to every task at each training moment. Probe families search per task: binary search finds a workable depth in logarithmic probes; enumeration just tries everything. Both share a hidden assumption: for any given task there exists one optimal depth worth locating. item.title: Gated Recurrent Transformers: Expressive Depth through Recurrent Modulation
item.description: By Amr Hegazy, Amr Alanwar, Mostafa Elhoushi (The German University in Cairo; Technical University of Munich; Cerebras Systems) Gated Recurrent Transformers: Expressive Depth through Recurrent Modulation, by Amr Hegazy of the German University in Cairo, Amr Alanwar of the Technical University of Munich, and Mostafa Elhoushi of Cerebras Systems. The paper starts from a tension every large-model engineer knows: depth and parameters are rigidly coupled in a standard transformer, because every layer carries its own weights, so the memory bill grows exactly as fast as the expressivity. Weight tying breaks that coupling, but naive tying forces an identical transformation onto what are radically different representational stages, and the representation after the first recurrence is nothing like the one after the eighth, so a static shared layer collapses the very functional diversity that makes depth valuable. The paper grounds this in a framing worth repeating: a finite set of states applied iteratively is enough to compute anything computable, so the power of a reasoning system may lie in the depth of iteration rather than the breadth of parameters, and recurrent depth is the hidden-state analogue of test-time chain-of-thought, thinking longer within the residual stream instead of spending tokens. The paper's answer to the collapse problem is borrowed from an old idea: treat the hidden state across recurrences the way a GRU treats its state across time, and let a learned gate decide, element by element, how much of the shared block's output to absorb at each pass. The same weights become fixed in parameters but dynamic in behavior.

item.title: GigaBrain-0.7: Scaling Embodied Foundation Models to Emergent Capabilities with a Three-System Architecture
item.description: By Angen Ye, Axiang Sun, Can Jin (GigaAI) GigaBrain-0.7: Scaling Embodied Foundation Models to Emergent Capabilities with a Three-System Architecture, by Angen Ye, Axiang Sun, and Can Jin — the first three names of a large alphabetically ordered team at GigaAI. The paper describes an embodied foundation model built as three cooperating systems: a vision-language planner, a flow-matching action generator, and a world-model-based predictor that supplies imagined subgoal images and value signals to the controller. The team pretrained it on roughly thirty-seven thousand hours of robot and human manipulation data plus about two hundred seventy-two million vision-language samples, and argues that scale alone starts producing reliable behaviors that small models do not show. The framing question is worth restating because the whole paper hangs on it. Vision-language-action models have become the default recipe for generalist robots, but most systems are trained and evaluated at modest data scale on narrow task suites. The authors ask two things at once: does architectural design still matter once you scale heterogeneous pretraining data, and does real-robot competence improve smoothly or discontinuously as data grows. Their answer is that both hold: architecture choices change what scaling is worth, and several capabilities they care about — deformable-object folding, sustained contact tasks — barely work at small data fractions and become dependable only near full scale.

item.title: WeMM-Embedding: WeChat Multi-Modal Embedding Technical Report
item.description: By Junjie Zhou, Ke Mei, Lei Li (Tencent) WeMM-Embedding: WeChat Multi-Modal Embedding Technical Report, by Junjie Zhou, Ke Mei, and Lei Li — three co-first authors at WeChat Vision, part of Tencent. This is a family of universal multimodal embedding models at two, four, and nine billion parameters, built on natively multimodal Qwen3.5 backbones. The headline claims: the two-billion variant already beats prior leading eight-billion open models on the MMEB-v2 benchmark suite, and the nine-billion model posts an overall score of eighty point six, first on the official leaderboard as of August twenty-fourth, twenty twenty-six. Unlike many embedding reports, this one ships with production evidence — fourteen online A/B tests across WeChat recommendation and search, all consistent enough to roll out. Start with the representation interface, because it drives everything downstream. Any input is an optional task instruction followed by an ordered sequence of text, image, and video segments. The model appends a dedicated embedding token to the sequence and takes that token's final hidden state, L-two normalized, as the vector. Because attention stays causal and native, you can insert several embedding tokens at different positions and pull out multiple representations from one forward pass — their worked example places one token after a video's frames and another after its speech transcript, yielding a video-only vector and a joint video-plus-transcript vector simultaneously. Matryoshka Representation Learning handles dimension flexibility: truncate the vector to any supported width, renormalize, done, with all widths computable from a single forward pass. The release also includes the data construction pipeline and inference stack, so a team could in principle reproduce the family end to end rather than merely download weights. item.title: AutoSaddler: Automatic Harness Optimization with Durable Updates from Agent Execution Traces
item.description: By Sungho Park, Wonjoong Kim, Rongyuan Tan (POSTECH; KAIST; SUSTech; Microsoft) AutoSaddler: Automatic Harness Optimization with Durable Updates from Agent Execution Traces, by Sungho Park of POSTECH, Wonjoong Kim of KAIST, and Rongyuan Tan of Southern University of Science and Technology, with colleagues at Microsoft where the first author interned. The premise: language-model agents stay unreliable on long-horizon tasks partly because the scaffolding around the model — prompts, tool definitions, control flow — is hand-tuned folklore. AutoSaddler treats that harness as the thing to train: an offline optimization loop that runs the agent on mini-batches of tasks, diagnoses failed traces against the harness source code, generates targeted patches, keeps what validates, and remembers everything in a search graph. Across three agent benchmarks it lifts pass-at-one by nine to ten percentage points over well-regarded manual harnesses. The formal setup is borrowed straight from machine learning and worth stating because every design choice falls out of it. Executing an agent under harness parameters theta defines a distribution over traces and outputs; the objective is expected task metric over a task distribution, estimated empirically because each evaluation costs a rollout. Training splits into train, development, and test sets drawn from disjoint task groups — on the software benchmark, training uses one repository entirely, validation two others, testing three more — so measured gains reflect generalization rather than memorized repairs. Each iteration evaluates the current harness on a mini-batch, enters a diagnosis-and-patch session, verifies improvement on that batch, optionally checks the development set, then reflects and plans the next candidate.
