item.title: SecOPD: Mitigating Adaptive Prompt Injections by On-Policy Distillation
item.description: By Yibo Peng, Long Lian, David Wagner (UC Berkeley) SecOPD: Mitigating Adaptive Prompt Injections by On-Policy Distillation, by Yibo Peng, Long Lian, David Wagner, and Sizhe Chen at the University of California, Berkeley, with Wagner and Chen jointly supervising. The paper attacks a specific and widely repeated failure: model-level prompt-injection defenses trained with sequence-level feedback look strong on paper and then collapse under an adaptive attack that optimizes against them. The proposed fix changes only the training signal — per-token scores derived from the same model shown a clean version of each input — and with that single change, attack success rate against the strongest adaptive attack drops from ninety-four percent to nine. Start with the threat model, because the paper's scope is narrower than headlines suggest. A trusted user instruction sits in one message; untrusted external data — web pages, documents, tool outputs — sits in another, using a dedicated input message type added to the chat template. The adversary controls only the untrusted field and may embed any instruction there. The defended model should keep using external data as context while never obeying instructions inside it. This is indirect injection where the user is benign; the authors state plainly that jailbreaks, direct injections, and malicious-user attacks are out of scope. They also assume the system already knows which input parts are trusted, which sidesteps a hard open problem rather than solving it. Training pairs every clean example with an attacked twin differing only in whether an injection sits inside the untrusted field — most injections placed at its beginning or end, occasionally in completion style behind delimiters — so the two contexts remain otherwise identical. item.title: CyberFactory: Scaling Cyber Security Capabilities with Instances from the Wild
item.description: By Jian Yang, Haau-Sing Li, Shawn Guo (Beihang University; ELLIS; IQuest Research; Singapore Management University) CyberFactory: Scaling Cyber Security Capabilities with Instances from the Wild, by Jian Yang of Beihang University, Haau-Sing Li of ELLIS, and Shawn Guo of IQuest Research, with collaborators including a corresponding author at Singapore Management University. The paper's pitch is a full recipe rather than just weights: an open-source framework that converts public vulnerability records into executable, verifiable training tasks spanning proof-of-concept generation, vulnerability patching, and security question answering, then trains a model called OpenAegis on agentic trajectories grounded in those tasks. On the CyberGym reproduction benchmark under a one-hour-per-task budget, OpenAegis reaches fifty-eight point one percent pass-at-one — twenty-eight and a half points above its own Qwen 3.5 base checkpoint at the same size, and ahead of substantially larger frontier models evaluated under identical scaffolding. The evaluation target deserves explanation first because everything else serves it. A task asks the agent to produce a proof-of-concept input that reproduces a real vulnerability, given only a natural-language description and the codebase. Success is judged by a differential oracle: the input must trigger the sanitizer failure on the pre-patch build and leave the patched build unharmed. That two-sided check rules out inputs that crash for incidental reasons and makes success machine-checkable — no human grader, no string matching against an expected answer. Because the oracle is programmatic and decidable, the agent gets free verification feedback, which turns exploit construction into a propose, verify, refine loop rather than one-shot generation.

item.title: Recursive Experiential–Working Memory Evolution for Long-Horizon Agent Harnesses
item.description: By Zhaochen Yu, Yingcheng Wu, Zhenfei Yin (NUS; Stanford University; University of Oxford; Princeton University) Recursive Experiential–Working Memory Evolution for Long-Horizon Agent Harnesses, by Zhaochen Yu of the National University of Singapore, Yingcheng Wu of Stanford University, and Zhenfei Yin of the University of Oxford, with senior authors at Princeton University. The system is called Recuris, and its claim to novelty is a disciplined version of recursive self-improvement: nothing about the language model changes, ever. Instead an external memory-control layer — skills, working-state schema, invocation policy, verification checks — evolves through a validation-gated loop while everything else stays frozen. Across four long-horizon benchmarks and ten models, that layer improves task success in thirty-five of thirty-seven completed pairings, including lifting Claude Opus five from seventy-two point four to eighty-seven point nine percent on a retail tool-use benchmark. The two design moves deserve separate treatment because they carry separate lessons. First, how memory gets used during a task. Prior experiential-memory harnesses retrieve skills against either the initial instruction or the entire chat history, and both degrade as execution unfolds — instructions go stale, histories fill with completed steps and noise. Recuris maintains instead a compact structured working state where each goal records content, status — pending, done, or blocked — supporting evidence, and any blocker. The crucial discipline is evidential: goals move to done only when an explicit checker predicate confirms completion from the environment's response, not from the model's own claim. Invoking a skill or attempting a tool call is explicitly defined as not being completion evidence. item.title: Apodex 1.1: Scaling Agentic Intelligence for Complex Work
item.description: By Apodex Team, B. An, B. Li (Apodex) Apodex 1.1: Scaling Agentic Intelligence for Complex Work, by the 71-author Apodex Team, with B. An, B. Li, and colleagues at Apodex, a company that publishes model weights on Hugging Face and runs an API platform alongside its research reports. The technical report frames one capability as the actual target: working capability, defined as sustained, verifiable progress toward a real-world objective. The argument is that general-purpose models reason and summarize adequately, but complex professional work requires sustained interaction with files, information sources, and executable code, plus state maintenance across failures and delivery of artifacts that survive checking. The paper scales that capability along two declared axes, Environment Scaling and Agentic Coordination Scaling, and reports results across professional work, finance, science, mathematics, search, and coding. Prior agentic systems mostly optimize isolated responses or single-domain loops. ReAct established the reasoning, action, observation cycle; SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench grade repository and command-line work; APEX-Agents grades long-horizon cross-application tasks designed by investment bankers, consultants, and lawyers; deep-research systems handle open-ended information seeking. What is missing in most of that line of work is a single model and runtime where file, search, and code execution compose inside one policy, with coordination treated as a trained behavior rather than a prompted wrapper. Apodex 1.0 was this group's earlier verification-centric agent team. Version 1.1 keeps the architecture and changes three things materially: broader verifiable training environments, an explicit external task board with asynchronous human intervention, and a dedicated synthesis stage separated from team execution.

item.title: TLive-Omni: An Omni-Modal Understanding Model for E-Commerce Live Streaming
item.description: By Yibo Hu; Yu Qian; Mao Gu; Yingfan Tao (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) **Cold open:** Picture a livestream that never stops. A host talks for six straight hours about a moisturizer, holds it up to the camera, peels off the label so you can read the ingredients, while hundreds of viewers type questions faster than any human moderator could answer. When does the discount code appear? Does it work on sensitive skin? What did the price look like half an hour ago? Every fact a viewer needs lives somewhere in that torrent of speech, pixels, and scrolling text — and no single modality carries it alone. Taming that torrent is the goal of TLive-Omni, a new system from Yibo Hu, Yu Qian, Mao Gu, Yingfan Tao, and their colleagues at Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba. The paper — TLive-Omni: An Omni-Modal Understanding Model for E-Commerce Live Streaming — appeared on arXiv on August twenty-first, twenty twenty-six, under the plain byline TLive-Omni Team. With it came two open checkpoints, at four billion and nine billion parameters, published on Hugging Face and GitHub. Here is what they built, how they trained it, and where the numbers genuinely stand. Under the hood this is a text-output omni model: a Qwen3.5 vision-language backbone, extended with the audio transformer encoder from Qwen3-Omni, grafted into the same embedding space through a lightweight two-layer aligner. That audio encoder was pretrained from scratch on twenty million hours of audio and compresses speech to roughly thirteen tokens per second, which is what makes long recordings affordable. The whole system accepts up to two hundred fifty-six thousand multimodal tokens of context — hours of stream in a single pass.

item.title: MobilePA-Bench: Benchmarking Mobile Planner Agents on Complex Real-World Tasks
item.description: By Yi Zhu, Xiongwei Wu, Qiyi Wang (MAI Team, Alibaba Token Foundry) MobilePA-Bench: Benchmarking Mobile Planner Agents on Complex Real-World Tasks, by Yi Zhu, Xiongwei Wu, and Qiyi Wang of the MAI Team at Alibaba Token Foundry. The first two authors contributed equally, Feida Zhu and Yiran Zhong led the project, and the entire apparatus is open-sourced: 1,705 interactive tasks, 212 simulated mobile tools, the sandbox, and the evaluation harness. The premise is narrow and worth stating precisely. As phone assistants mature into agents that place calls, book travel, and restructure device settings on a user's behalf, there has been no agreed instrument for measuring whether a planner actually finishes such jobs. This paper builds one and reports what happens when thirteen frontier models are pushed through it. Existing benchmarks split into two camps, and the authors document blind spots in both. GUI-centric suites — AndroidWorld, OSWorld, WindowsAgentArena, MobiBench — put a vision-language model in front of screenshots and grade pixel-level navigation. That exercises perception, but tapping icons is a fraction of what a competent phone agent does, and rendering-heavy environments carry latencies that make them impractical for reinforcement learning rollouts. Static function-calling suites — the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard, ToolBench, DroidCall, AppBench — sit at the opposite extreme: the model emits a JSON blob and an answer key grades the string, offline, with no live state. Nothing executes, so runtime exceptions, permission boundaries, and call dependencies never enter the picture. TAU-bench adds multi-turn transactions but models business logic rather than operating-system dependencies. item.title: Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness
item.description: By Seth Karten, Alex L. Zhang, Kevin Thomas (Princeton University; Prime Intellect; MIT) Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness, by Seth Karten of Princeton University and Prime Intellect, Alex L. Zhang of Prime Intellect and MIT, and Kevin Thomas of Prime Intellect, together with additional co-authors from those groups. The paper presents an open-source agent harness built around a persistent IPython execution layer, recursive language-model subagents, direct agent-to-agent messaging, and a versioned store of prompts, memories, skills, and subagent specifications, and reports evaluations spanning interactive reasoning, long-context coding, GPU kernel generation, emulator construction, and multi-day autonomous runs. The framing: a language model is a bounded sequential processor whose next decision conditions only on fixed weights and whatever sits in the active context. A harness supplies everything else. The authors organize the resulting state into four levels: model weights as level zero, active context as level one, a persistent REPL plus recursive subagents as level two, and disk-backed history, artifacts, memories, skills, prompts, and subagent specifications as level three. Their measurement argument is the motivating claim. A model should fail an evaluation because the task exceeds its capability, not because the harness dropped state, restricted useful actions, miscounted resources, or terminated prematurely. The components existed separately before. Recursive Language Models made context handling programmable; Continual Harness made prompts and skills revisable from trajectory history. What was missing was one substrate integrating both with persistence, recovery, verification, and unified accounting, and that integration is the contribution here.

item.title: RISE: Adaptive Imagination for World Action Models
item.description: By Hongbo Lu, Liang Yao, Chenghao He (COWARobot Co. Ltd; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Hohai University) RISE: Adaptive Imagination for World Action Models, by Hongbo Lu, Liang Yao, Chenghao He, together with Hao Han, Fan Liu, Wenlong Liao, Tao He, and Pai Peng at COWARobot Co. Ltd, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and Hohai University. The paper appeared on the Hugging Face daily papers list for August 25, 2026 with twenty-three upvotes, and ships a project page, a code repository, and a dataset release. The claim is narrow and implementable: World Action Models waste computation by granting every driving scene the same imagination budget, and a small learned scheduler that decides, step by step, whether to keep imagining the future or stop and plan, buys better planning at lower rollout cost. Context first. End-to-end driving is moving away from direct trajectory regression toward policies that reason about the future before acting. World Action Models predict world evolution and judge actions by their consequences rather than by the current observation alone. At inference there are three established arrangements of that computation. Shared-backbone designs run prediction and planning from one representation, an imagine-and-plan scheme. Cascaded designs complete an entire future rollout before handing it to the planner, imagine-then-plan. A third family removes test-time imagination and plans directly from the observation. The paper's observation is that all three fix the schedule globally: nothing reassesses, after each predicted step, whether the partial future built so far already supports a good plan. item.title: ARC: Fair Relative Advantage Comparison in Open-Ended Real-World Interaction
item.description: By Yongqi Tong, Tan Li Hui Faith, Choy Zhen Wen Marcus (Ant International) ARC: Fair Relative Advantage Comparison in Open-Ended Real-World Interaction, by Yongqi Tong, Tan Li Hui Faith, and Choy Zhen Wen Marcus, equal-contribution first authors at Ant International, with Zhou Jin, Kewei Fu, Jiang-Ming Yang, Jianshe Li, and Xin Zhang as coauthors. The paper addresses a specific failure mode in group-based reinforcement learning for agents: when one rollout group mixes different conversation strategies, relative advantages stop measuring response quality and start measuring whatever interaction style the reward model happens to prefer. First the problem, because the mechanism only makes sense against it. Group-based methods such as GRPO sample several responses per prompt, subtract the group mean reward, and use the centered value as the advantage. That signal is interpretable only when the compared rollouts are behaviorally comparable. In open-ended interaction they often are not: for the same dialogue state the agent may answer directly from memory, ask for clarification first, stream progress updates while tools run, or restate intent and confirm before an irreversible action. All of these can be task-appropriate. Reward models carry exposure, length, and style bias, so when a group spans qualitatively different behaviors, the centered reward absorbs region-specific reward preference along with genuine quality differences. The authors formalize this as a fairness property: a reward model is delta-fair if two equally good responses following different strategies score within delta of each other, and they argue real reward models violate it systematically in agent settings where interaction appropriateness lacks ground truth. item.title: EnvHarness: Awakening Static Worlds for Agent Learning
item.description: By Chengsong Huang, Zifeng Wang, Rujun Han (Washington University in St. Louis; Google Cloud AI Research; Google Cloud; University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill) EnvHarness: Awakening Static Worlds for Agent Learning, by Chengsong Huang, Zifeng Wang, and Rujun Han, with fourteen more authors including Burak Gokturk, Tomas Pfister, and Chen-Yu Lee. Huang did this work while interning at Google Cloud AI Research, and the affiliation list covers Washington University in St. Louis, Google Cloud AI Research, Google Cloud, and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Here is the premise, and it is a reasonable one. As language models become agents, the scarce resource for training shifts from curated text data to interactive environments. Those environments are hand-built: someone hardcodes interaction logic and a verifier, and the result behaves identically whether it faces a novice or a competent policy. Two failure modes follow. A static environment cannot target the specific weaknesses of the policy you actually have, and once the policy learns to solve its existing tasks, the environment has nothing left to teach. Automated environment generation exists as an alternative, with systems like GenEnv simulating environments and their feedback inside a model, VeriEnv synthesizing executable environments programmatically, and SWE-smith generating new task instances within an existing benchmark. But those pipelines are domain-specific, each built separately for web navigation, programming, or tool use, and because both tasks and verifiers come out of a model, teams over-generate and filter heavily without ever guaranteeing correctness. EnvHarness takes a different position: stop authoring new environments, and reshape the ones you already trust.

item.title: FACET: Preserving Source Intent and Executable State in Terminal Task Synthesis
item.description: By Kou Shi, Zun Wang, Qisheng Su (MoE Key Lab of BIPC, University of Science and Technology of China; Shanghai AI Laboratory; Fudan University) FACET: Preserving Source Intent and Executable State in Terminal Task Synthesis, by Kou Shi, Zun Wang, and Qisheng Su, with ten more authors including Feng Zhao as corresponding author. The affiliations are the MoE Key Lab of BIPC at the University of Science and Technology of China, Shanghai AI Laboratory, and Fudan University. The problem this paper attacks is concrete: training terminal agents needs scalable, executable supervision, and every synthesized terminal task is a tightly coupled bundle of an instruction, an initialized environment, a reference solution, and an executable verifier, packaged in the Harbor format that Terminal-Bench uses. If those artifacts are generated under inconsistent assumptions you get tasks that cannot be solved or that grade incorrectly. Two failure mechanisms dominate multi-stage synthesis pipelines. First, information loss: source material rich in capabilities, dependencies, intermediate states, input-output contracts, and procedural constraints gets progressively compressed into a simplified task description, preserving only a fraction of the available structure. Second, artifact drift: an instruction references a file never realized in the environment, a solution assumes a different schema or dependency version, or a verifier tests a state the generated task cannot produce. Passing textual specifications between generation stages mitigates neither problem, because text is not a shared realized state.

item.title: SWE-bench Science: Can Coding Agents Resolve Engineering Tasks in Science?
item.description: By Zhipeng Xu, Jiahao Lu, Yining Zheng (Shanghai Innovation Institute; Fudan University) SWE-bench Science: Can Coding Agents Resolve Engineering Tasks in Science?, by Zhipeng Xu, Jiahao Lu, and Yining Zheng, with Yuxin Wang and Xipeng Qiu as corresponding authors, all affiliated with the Shanghai Innovation Institute and Fudan University. item.title: Repo0: Design-Driven Zero-to-All Code Generation
item.description: By Silin Chen, Haoyi Teng, Xiaodong Gu (Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Chongqing University) Repo0: Design-Driven Zero-to-All Code Generation, by Silin Chen and Haoyi Teng as equal first authors, Xiaodong Gu as corresponding author, with Yuling Shi, Jiale Huang, Yongpan Wang, Hongyu Zhang, and Haibing Guan. The affiliations are Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Chongqing University. The setting is zero-to-all code generation: an agent receives natural-language requirements and must construct an entire software project from nothing while maintaining a modular repository architecture throughout. Most existing systems quietly assume the opposite, that component boundaries, package organization, and dependency graphs are already given, which is why repository-completion work looks so much better than it should. The authors' diagnosis of prior systems, including RPG, the strongest graph-based baseline, is that they treat software design as a static artifact: a perfect architectural blueprint generated in one initial planning stage, then rigidly executed. Anyone who has shipped software knows the blueprint is wrong by the time implementation starts; generated code reveals whether planned components were ever cohesive or whether dependency edges are entangled. Repo0's answer is continuous structural evolution around an explicit architectural state, instantiated as what they call a Dual-DAG. Two directed acyclic graphs plus an alignment relation. The requirement-level DAG holds high-level requirements decomposed into sub-requirements, and its edges encode functional coordination: two requirements logically used together and needing joint consideration for behavior, inputs, and outputs. item.title: FlashPrefill V2: Block-Sparse Prefill Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving
item.description: By Qihang Fan, Huaibo Huang, Zhiying Wu (MAIS and NLPR, CASIA; UCAS; WeChat, Tencent) FlashPrefill V2: Block-Sparse Prefill Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving, by Qihang Fan, Huaibo Huang, and Zhiying Wu, with Bingning Wang as project leader and Ran He. The affiliations are the Institute of Automation of the Chinese Academy of Sciences through its MAIS and NLPR labs, the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, and WeChat at Tencent; the first author completed the work during an internship at WeChat. Context for the audience: attention cost during prefill grows with the square of sequence length, and every training-free sparse-attention method lives or dies on three practical questions. Does accuracy survive aggressive sparsity? Is the kernel competitive with current dense implementations rather than last generation's? And does it work inside a real serving stack with paged KV cache and continuous batching? Their previous FlashPrefill answered none of those fully. It discovered patterns instantaneously using mean-pooled keys and max-based dynamic thresholding, avoiding the global sorting that Top-k selection requires, but accuracy degraded without bound under extreme sparsity, the kernel was built on FlashAttention-2's execution model, which leaves Hopper tensor-core throughput on the table, and it assumed a contiguous KV layout incompatible with any modern serving framework. V2 addresses exactly these three gaps.

item.title: FlowEvo: Self-Evolving Agents through the Co-Evolution of Workflows and Executable Skills
item.description: By Zeyu Ren, Ling Yue, Ran Li (Southeast University; Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute; The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology) FlowEvo: Self-Evolving Agents through the Co-Evolution of Workflows and Executable Skills, by Zeyu Ren, Ling Yue, and Ran Li, with Yishu Wang, Shengxiang Xu, Hanmo Liu, Shaowu Pan, and Shimin Di. The affiliations are Southeast University, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, and the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. The gap this paper identifies is real and worth articulating precisely. Workflow-based agents construct procedures at inference time: decomposition, tool calls, code generation, checking, repair. But whatever structure a successful episode discovers gets discarded when the episode ends. Skill libraries preserve reusable routines as executable objects, yet they are typically assembled offline for a fixed task distribution rather than growing from the agent's own problem solving. Text memories such as Agent Workflow Memory sit in between: they describe what worked but cannot be invoked or validated, so reuse still depends on the model re-deriving the procedure from prose. FlowEvo is a training-free framework that closes this loop: successful workflows are compiled into callable skill records stored in a persistent bank, and those skills feed back into later workflow construction either through direct execution or as structured context. Model weights never change.

item.title: Zetta ζ: An Efficient Closed-Loop Embodied Harness for Self-Evolving Physical Intelligence
item.description: By Xin Ding, Liang Mi, Mingzhe Huang (Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University; Z-Trans AI) The paper is "Zetta Zeta: An Efficient Closed-Loop Embodied Harness for Self-Evolving Physical Intelligence." Yes, the Greek letter zeta is genuinely in the title. The first three authors are Xin Ding, Liang Mi, and Mingzhe Huang, leading a fourteen-person list from the Institute for AI Industry Research at Tsinghua University — AIR for short — together with Z-Trans AI. It sits at the top of the day's daily list with 145 upvotes, so a lot of people want this story to be true. Whether it holds up is a fair question, and we will get there. The problem is familiar to anyone who has shipped a robot policy. Vision-language-action models keep failing once they leave the curated evaluation suite, because the things that made training work — dense supervision, verifiable rewards, clean resets — stop existing at deployment time. The usual response is to freeze everything at ship date and route observed failures back to the vendor for the next release cycle, which means every fix waits months and every regression risks undoing old ones. The authors argue the mistake is treating the whole stack as one frozen object. Their split is cleaner: the base policy stays frozen, and the harness around it — runtime critics, recovery routines, rollout plumbing — becomes the part that evolves, using nothing but the stream of episodes the robot already produces during ordinary operation. No new labels, no human-in-the-loop repair queue, no fine-tuning runs that could destabilize the skills the policy already has.

item.title: SemaPLC: A Project-Grounded, Verification-Gated Agent Harness for PLC Code Generation
item.description: By Yanlun Tu, Huacan Wang, Ziyue Zhou (Midea AIRC; KUKA; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Zhejiang University) The paper is "SemaPLC: A Project-Grounded, Verification-Gated Agent Harness for PLC Code Generation." The first three authors are Yanlun Tu, Huacan Wang, and Ziyue Zhou, heading a thirteen-person list that spans Midea AIRC, KUKA, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and Zhejiang University. Note who is on that list: Midea builds appliances at planetary scale, and KUKA builds industrial robots that weld cars and move pallets — these are people whose code, if subtly wrong, stops actual factories or worse. With 116 upvotes it is the second most-upvoted paper of the day, and unlike everything else in today's lineup, nothing here touches transformers at all. No new model, no fine-tuning trick, no benchmark of yet another chatbot. Just an argument about how software agents ought to be allowed to finish their work. The subject is programmable logic controllers — PLCs — the rugged, deterministic computers that run assembly lines, water treatment plants, HVAC systems, and chemical dosing pumps. They are not glamorous, but civilization quietly depends on them, and they have a programming culture all their own: cycle-time budgets, hard real-time constraints, interlock logic where the wrong line of code can physically hurt someone. Large language models can already generate individual program organization units — POUs, essentially the functions of control logic — at usable quality for isolated tasks. What they cannot reliably do, and what this paper takes on, is the part that actually matters in production: making newly generated logic integrate into an existing PLC project, respecting its established variables, device configurations, naming conventions, and safety interlocks, and then verifying that the combined result behaves correctly before anyone lets it near hardware. item.title: Co-RL: Unsupervised Reasoning Emerges from Diverse Cohort in Multi-agent RL
item.description: By Yunhao Yang, Yuexin Bian, Yunjie Tian (Johns Hopkins University; UC San Diego; University of Exeter) The paper is "Co-RL: Unsupervised Reasoning Emerges from Diverse Cohort in Multi-agent RL." The first three authors are Yunhao Yang, Yuexin Bian, and Yunjie Tian, leading a nine-author group spread across Johns Hopkins University, UC San Diego, and the University of Exeter, with a couple of independent researchers mixed in. At 92 upvotes it sits third on the day, and its promise is the one everybody wants: reasoning improvements from reinforcement learning with zero ground-truth labels. To see the problem, start from the standard recipe. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains models on problems with checkable answers — math with known solutions, code with known outputs — and it works embarrassingly well. The catch is that verifiable answers require humans to have produced them, and as capabilities advance past what people can reliably evaluate, the supervision supply line thins exactly where you want to push. Self-rewarding methods respond by letting the model grade its own completions, no labels needed. The trouble, documented repeatedly, is what happens when a student grades its own exam: the model drifts toward confidently rewarding its own errors, and training collapses into elaborate self-flattery. The most-cited cautionary example is TTRL, which leans on majority voting over the model's own samples — workable early, but as training progresses the votes simply ratify whatever the model already believes, so the pseudo-labels freeze around the model's initial competence instead of stretching it. Every label-free scheme has to answer the same uncomfortable question: where does genuinely new corrective signal enter the system? If the only source of judgment is the model being judged, the honest answer is nowhere.

item.title: OmniScientist: An Omni-Modal Omni-Discipline AI Scientist
item.description: By Bobo Li, Hao Fei, Tianjie Ju, Mong-Li Lee, Wynne Hsu (National University of Singapore; University of Oxford) Hello everyone, and welcome back. Today's paper is "OmniScientist: An Omni-Modal Omni-Discipline AI Scientist," by Bobo Li, Hao Fei, Tianjie Ju, Mong-Li Lee, and Wynne Hsu, a collaboration between the National University of Singapore and the University of Oxford, and it sits near the top of today's community picks with eighty-nine upvotes. The pitch is an autonomous research system that does not merely read papers and write code — it looks at raw scientific evidence directly: micrographs, waveforms, satellite imagery, audio recordings, three-dimensional point clouds, time-lapse video. The authors argue that everything currently calling itself an AI scientist shares a specific blind spot, and that blind spot is where the actual science lives. To see the argument, look at what existing systems actually consume. Automated research frameworks have gotten genuinely impressive at orchestrating workflows: generate hypotheses, plan experiments, execute code, draft manuscripts. But inspect the input side and you find text, code, class labels, or precomputed summaries — someone else already did the looking, the summarizing, and crucially the deciding about what mattered. The spatial relation between two regions of a tissue slide, the temporal drift across hours of a sensor trace, the cross-channel coupling in a multivariate signal, the procedural detail of how an experiment was physically performed: these are scientifically decisive, and they are exactly what never survives conversion into a scalar feature or a caption. The authors' phrase for it is that workflow coverage does not provide access to the full evidence on which discovery depends. A scientist who never touches their own data is not doing science; they are doing literature review with extra steps. Whether

item.title: Training Chemical Plausibility-Aware Large Language Models for Single-Step Retrosynthesis
item.description: By Bogdan Zagribelnyy, Ivan Ilin, Nikita Bondarev, Maksim Kuznetsov, Mathieu Reymond, Vladimir Aladinskiy, Alex Aliper, Alex Zhavoronkov (Insilico Medicine — Abu Dhabi, Montreal, and Hong Kong) Welcome back, everyone. Today's paper is "Training Chemical Plausibility-Aware Large Language Models for Single-Step Retrosynthesis," by Bogdan Zagribelnyy, Ivan Ilin, Nikita Bondarev, Maksim Kuznetsov, Mathieu Reymond, Vladimir Aladinskiy, Alex Aliper, and Alex Zhavoronkov of Insilico Medicine, with labs spanning Abu Dhabi, Montreal, and Hong Kong. It carries thirty-three upvotes on today's board, and underneath the chemistry it is making a methodological argument the broader ML community should hear: some problems are intrinsically one-to-many, and forcing them into single-answer evaluation quietly breaks both your training signal and your benchmarks. Here is the setup. Retrosynthesis asks the question a chemist faces when staring at a target molecule: what known reaction could produce this? It is the core step of computer-aided synthesis planning, and drug discovery lives or dies on synthetic accessibility — designing a compound nobody can manufacture is designing nothing. The structural difficulty is that the answer is rarely unique: a target molecule typically admits many valid precursor sets through many different reaction types, all chemically plausible, several industrially sensible. Single-answer protocols — predict the one right disconnection, score against one ground truth — punish diversity and reward memorizing the majority route. The authors' response is Top-K prompting, used consistently at both training and inference: the model learns to emit a ranked set of plausible disconnections rather than a lone guess, which matches the task's actual geometry instead of fighting it. item.title: Training Leaves Traces: Centered Residual Signatures for Language Model Lineage Verification
item.description: By Aman Singh Thakur, Rayan Khoury (Amazon; Massachusetts Institute of Technology) Welcome back. Today's paper is "Training Leaves Traces: Centered Residual Signatures for Language Model Lineage Verification," by Aman Singh Thakur of Amazon and Rayan Khoury of MIT, sitting with eighteen upvotes on today's board — modest numbers for what might be the most quietly consequential question of the day: given two open-weight model checkpoints, can you tell from the weights alone whether one descends from the other? No training logs, no data, no behavioral testing, no metadata to trust or distrust. Just the tensors. The motivation comes from how model distribution actually works now. Open-weight models move through supply chains rather than as single releases: a base checkpoint gets fine-tuned, quantized, pruned, adapted with low-rank updates, merged with other models, renamed, and redistributed — sometimes documented, often not, and occasionally deliberately obscured. The existing verification toolbox is embarrassingly thin. Cryptographic hashes break the moment any weight changes, which means every legitimate fine-tune invalidates the hash. Metadata and licensing files require honesty from whoever relabeled the model, which is exactly the resource an adversary controls. Behavioral fingerprints — probing outputs to guess ancestry — are confounded by distillation: two models that behave alike need not share a single weight, and two models sharing every weight can be made to behave differently. The paper's framing is precise about what is being claimed: data-free, white-box lineage verification, asking whether ancestry leaves a structural trace in weights themselves that survives benign modification and cannot be removed without breaking the model.

item.title: Demystifying Agent Skills: Why They Work—Until They Don't
item.description: By Zhiyuan Jiang, Fangrui Huang, Hanwen Xing (Princeton University; UC San Diego; Stanford University; University of Southern California; Johns Hopkins University) Demystifying Agent Skills: Why They Work—Until They Don't. First authors Zhiyuan Jiang, Fangrui Huang, and Hanwen Xing, working across Princeton University, UC San Diego, Stanford University, the University of Southern California, and Johns Hopkins University. The paper asks a question most skill evaluations skip entirely: when do agent skills actually help, why do they work, and where do they fail. If you maintain SKILL.md-style packages in production agents, this is a measurement paper worth your attention. Here is the gap being addressed. Skills are structured knowledge packages injected into an agent's environment at inference time. Existing evaluations report aggregate task success with and without skills, which tells you nothing about mechanism. A skill could win because it injects missing facts, because it stabilizes execution, or by accident. Those three explanations imply very different engineering investments, and aggregate success rates cannot distinguish them. The study design is the strongest part of the paper. The authors compare three conditions built from identical source material: Raw, meaning no prior experience; Workflow Memory, meaning cleaned execution traces from prior runs handed to the agent directly; and Skill, meaning a standardized SKILL.md document distilled from exactly the same traces. Because Workflow Memory and Skill are constructed from the same underlying trajectories, any difference between them isolates the effect of representation rather than the effect of having seen past experience. item.title: FreeToken: Efficient Edge-Native MoE Serving with Bandwidth-Adaptive Execution
item.description: By Shuo Yang, Xiaoze Fan, Melissa Pan (UC Berkeley; University of Texas at Austin; MIT; University of Michigan) FreeToken: Efficient Edge-Native MoE Serving with Bandwidth-Adaptive Execution. Shuo Yang, Xiaoze Fan, and Melissa Pan led the work, with the author group spanning UC Berkeley, the University of Texas at Austin, MIT, and the University of Michigan—the PDF's first page lists correspondence through Berkeley and UT Austin addresses. The claim: a serving stack co-designed for consumer hardware can run frontier-scale mixture-of-experts models interactively on machines people already own. Skeptical? So was I. The numbers are specific enough to check. The problem first. Open-weight frontier models like GLM-5.2 at 753 billion parameters and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 284 billion parameters with 13 billion active per token are free to download and expensive to run. They assume datacenter GPUs whose clusters cost millions of dollars, and hosted APIs remain burdensome for individuals as agentic applications multiply inference demand. Meanwhile over one hundred million consumer machines have discrete GPUs—Steam alone reports more than 200 million monthly active users with discrete NVIDIA GPUs on roughly 72 percent of surveyed systems. Mixture-of-experts architectures make edge serving plausible because each token activates a small subset of experts—DeepSeek-V4-Flash routes to 6 of 256 experts in each of its 43 layers—but existing engines waste that sparsity in three distinct ways.

item.title: ASI-Bench: At the Dawn of Artificial Superintelligence
item.description: By Junwei Zhou, Zhen Sun, Binyu Li (Tsinghua University; University of Michigan; MIT; Harvard University) ASI-Bench: At the Dawn of Artificial Superintelligence. Core authors Junwei Zhou, Zhen Sun, and Binyu Li, from a large collaboration spanning Tsinghua University, the University of Michigan, MIT, Harvard University, Carnegie Mellon University, and several other institutions. The title oversells it; the benchmark does not. What this paper actually delivers is a controlled measurement of how fast frontier agents fall apart when you withdraw human methodological guidance, and that measurement is worth your time. The premise: today's AI mostly learns, compresses, and applies existing human knowledge. Benchmarks test whether systems produce correct answers from learned knowledge or complete tasks under heavy human specification. Nobody jointly measures innovative exploration—choosing how to attack an open research problem—and autonomous scientific execution across general domains, within one project, with guidance progressively removed. Existing options each cover a slice: Humanity's Last Exam is academic question answering; Terminal-Bench is terminal tasks; ScienceAgentBench is scientific analysis under largely fixed workflows; PaperBench is research replication; MLE-Bench is machine-learning engineering; RE-Bench is AI R&D; DiscoveryBench and SciCode cover data-driven discovery and scientific coding. All provide a fixed task specification. None asks whether the agent could have constructed the workflow itself, none spans general scientific domains at project level, and none varies guidance within the same research problem—so a high score can mean genuine discovery or faithful procedure-following, and the two are indistinguishable in the aggregate.

item.title: Embodied-Navigator: Point, Think, Memorize, and Align for Efficient Navigation
item.description: By Hongyan Feng, Sunlai Chen, Xuanyu Liu (Zhejiang University; Zhejiang Humanoid Robot Innovation Center) Embodied-Navigator: Point, Think, Memorize, and Align for Efficient Navigation. First authors Hongyan Feng, Sunlai Chen, and Xuanyu Liu, from the OmniAl Group of the ACES Lab at Zhejiang University together with the Zhejiang Humanoid Robot Innovation Center. The system is called TAMP-Nav: Point, Think, Memorize, Align. It reports 66.2 percent success on R2R-CE validation-unseen with a tenth of the training trajectories of some competitors, and it runs inference in about half the time per task. Those efficiency numbers are the real story here. Three bottlenecks motivate the design. First, the geometric gap: vision-language models are pretrained on 2D image-text pairs, but vision-and-language navigation forces them to emit low-level atomic actions like turn left thirty degrees or to regress 3D coordinates, which demands implicit geometric transformations they were never trained to perform and produces spatial hallucinations with poor sample efficiency. Second, the reasoning-efficiency dilemma: chain-of-thought improves high-level planning but existing models trigger it at every step or at fixed intervals, multiplying inference latency for marginal gains. Third, memory: keeping full visual history causes attention dilution and overflow, while discarding history or decaying it loses critical information, and most architectures carry no explicit spatio-temporal coordinates organizing what they keep.

item.title: AVA-Encoder: Towards Agent-Native Video Representation Learning
item.description: By Chuyue Li, Jinpeng Yu, Haozhe Wang (Qwen Business Unit of Alibaba; ShanghaiTech University; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology) AVA-Encoder: Towards Agent-Native Video Representation Learning. First authors Chuyue Li, Jinpeng Yu, and Haozhe Wang, from the Qwen Business Unit of Alibaba, ShanghaiTech University, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, the Institute of Computing Technology, and Southeast University. The problem: video creation agents cannot learn filmmaking from finished films, because a rendered video is not an operable record of the decisions that produced it—scripts, characters, shots, camera language, pacing, and audio design are coupled across space and time in ways the finished pixels do not expose. The proposal is to turn films into structured knowledge graphs that agents can read, query, edit, and reconstruct from—and to use reconstruction error itself as the training signal. The task formulation is an agentic auto-encoder. Three parts. An Agentic Video Encoder governed by a policy implemented as three distinct system prompts covering film-level, shot-level, and keyframe-level understanding, with inter-level context injection propagating information across granularities. A bottleneck that is not a neural embedding but a Film Knowledge Graph. And a fixed decoder: a static rendering pipeline calling frozen generation models as tools, taking reference keyframes and shot-prompt descriptions from the graph and rendering shots sequentially. Because the decoder never changes, any difference in reconstruction quality measures the representation. That is the entire evaluation philosophy—reconstruction fidelity as a proxy for representation faithfulness.

item.title: Agent Lightning v1.0: Towards Harnessed Agentic RL
item.description: By Zhiyuan He, Siwei Zhang, Zhiwen Zhou (Microsoft; Fudan University; Zhejiang University; University of Edinburgh) Agent Lightning v1.0: Towards Harnessed Agentic RL. First authors Zhiyuan He, Siwei Zhang, and Zhiwen Zhou, from Microsoft, Fudan University, Zhejiang University, and the University of Edinburgh. This paper does two things: it names and systematically characterizes a failure-prone regime—reinforcement learning on agents that run inside their own deployment harnesses—and it ships a roughly 3,500-line framework fixing the identified problems, with a coding-agent result that deserves scrutiny: Qwen3.5-9B improving on SWE-bench Verified from 41.8 to 56.4 percent using reinforcement learning alone on about 6,000 examples. Terminology first. Traditional agentic RL puts the environment loop inside the trainer: prompt tokens, action tokens, observation tokens concatenate into one Markov chain—prompt at step t equals the previous prompt plus the previous action plus the tokenized observation—one training sample per rollout. Harnessed agentic RL means the deploy-time harness—mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, Hermes—owns context construction, tool execution, and control flow, while the training engine observes only LLM request-response pairs crossing an API boundary. Both regimes fit partially observable Markov decision processes, but the latent state now includes harness state, and the policy sees separately constructed prompts per call. The proxy-based disaggregation came from the original Agent Lightning; verl Uni-Agent, AReaL 2.0, slime v0.3.0, and Polar have since adopted it. The contribution here is showing that this paradigm silently breaks four assumptions every standard trainer makes.

item.title: StateM: Reaching 95.3% Raw Accuracy, or a $15 Frontier Run, on Terminal-Bench 2.1 via Harness Scaling
item.description: By Ziheng Qin, Yaxin Lu, Zhangyang Atlas Wang (Somewhere on the Earth) StateM: Reaching 95.3 percent raw accuracy, or a $15 frontier run, on Terminal-Bench 2.1 via harness scaling. That is arXiv 2608.15089, from Ziheng Qin, Yaxin Lu, and Zhangyang Atlas Wang, joined by Kai Wang, who list their affiliation on the paper's first page as, literally, "Somewhere on the Earth." The work was done in the authors' personal time. The claim deserves attention anyway: without changing a single model weight, their agent runtime lifts GPT-5.5 xhigh from an 83.1 percent reference to 92.1 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and reaches 95.3 percent raw accuracy with GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh across 445 public-submission trials. Let me walk through what the system actually does, what the evidence does and does not cover, and where you should verify before adopting any of it. The premise is familiar to anyone who has babysat a long agent run: the underlying model clearly knows how to do each step, and the run still fails. The agent drifts off-plan, loses track of mutable task state, skips a required check, repeats an unproductive action, or stops before the deliverable is verifiably complete. Benchmarks score the completed job, not the fraction of steps the model understood. The paper frames the dominant alternative responses — more pretraining, more post-training data, longer reasoning, more agents — as orthogonal to its question: how much apparent model failure is actually failure of the surrounding harness, the layer that maintains state, constrains execution, verifies progress, and recovers from errors? They call systematically improving that layer harness scaling. item.title: Learn What's Left, Not What's Mastered: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization
item.description: By Yixuan Wang, Yifei Chen, Haichao Zhang (University of Florida; UC San Diego; Northeastern University; Northwestern University; Stanford University; Zillion Network; Universität Innsbruck) The paper is called Learn What's Left, Not What's Mastered: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization. The first three authors are Yixuan Wang, Yifei Chen, and Haichao Zhang, working with a nine-person roster that spans the University of Florida, UC San Diego, Northeastern University, Northwestern University, Stanford University together with Zillion Network, and the University of Innsbruck. The arXiv id is 2608.16072, dated August 18, 2026. Here is the problem they take on, and it is one of those problems that is obvious once stated. Group-relative policy optimization is now the de facto standard for post-training language model reasoners. You sample a group of rollouts per prompt, score them, subtract the group mean, divide by the group standard deviation, and push probabilities accordingly. It works because the baseline comes free from the group. The friction starts when you optimize several reward objectives at once — answer correctness, format compliance, a length penalty, a tool-use check, whatever your mixture happens to be. The universal practice is scalarization: sum the components into one reward, then run the usual group normalization on the total. That sum is where signal leaks out. Consider an objective the model has essentially mastered: every rollout in the group earns nearly the same score on it. Its within-group z-score is then pure sampling noise — tiny, directionless, occasionally nonzero for no reason at all. After scalarization, that noise still participates in the total advantage. item.title: HarnessEval-W: Agentifying the Evaluation of Visual Worlds
item.description: By Weiliang Chen, Haowen Sun, Jun Gao, et al. (MirroS Lab) Here is a question the world-model community has mostly been avoiding: how do you trust a score that comes with no explanation? Today's paper is HarnessEval-W: Agentifying the Evaluation of Visual Worlds — first authors Weiliang Chen, Haowen Sun, and Jun Gao, joined by co-authors including Jialong Wu, Jiangran Lyu, and Fangfu Liu in a forty-four-author collaboration whose benchmark and tooling ship publicly under the MirroS Lab organization. Their diagnosis is blunt. Current world-model evaluation compresses every prediction into metrics computed brute-force — pixel distances and classifier scores with no reasoning chain anyone can inspect. When two video-world models disagree about whether a cup stays on the table after a robot arm sweeps past, you receive two numbers and zero arguments. This paper's bet is that the evaluator itself should be an agent: something that investigates a generated rollout the way a careful reviewer investigates a manuscript, and leaves behind an evidence trail you can audit line by line. World models are becoming the planning core of embodied systems. An agent imagines forward — if I grasp here, the scene evolves there — and acts on the imagination. As these generators improve, the bottleneck moves from making predictions to grading them, and grading is where the field quietly cut corners. The standard toolkit measures observation overlap frame by frame, plus learned classifiers for physics plausibility. Those scores hide three distinct failure modes inside one average: did the model see what changed, did it predict the right dynamics, and did it remember the object three seconds later? item.title: UI-Mate: A Self-Evolving Companion for Computer-Use Agents
item.description: By Zihan Ding, Longxu Dou, Qi Gao, et al. (Tencent Hy Frontier Team) Today's paper is "UI-Mate: A Self-Evolving Companion for Computer-Use Agents," by Zihan Ding, Longxu Dou, Qi Gao, and twenty-six colleagues spanning Tencent's Hy Frontier team — twenty-nine authors in all. The pitch matches the name: rather than train yet another larger computer-use model, they built a companion that rides along with one, watches it operate, steps in the moment it stalls, and remembers every rescue so the next episode starts smarter. The headline claims are striking — 77.0 percent on OSWorld-Verified, reportedly the best open-weight result going, and a single demonstration doubling an agent's odds on tasks it currently fails. A computer-use agent is a language model driving a graphical interface the way you do: it reads a screenshot of the screen, decides what to do next, and then clicks, types, or scrolls. Benchmarks such as OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena grade these systems on genuine office work — editing spreadsheets, filing mail, changing system settings — inside live operating systems rather than toy replicas. Scores keep climbing, but the failure signature in the traces is remarkably stable: the agent behaves competently for twenty steps, then loops on the same wrong click, wanders off-target, or quits partway through, and it essentially never recovers by itself. item.title: ClawGym II: Exploring Black-Box RL on Agent Harness
item.description: By Huatong Song, Fei Bai, Ming Yang, et al. (Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China; IQuest Research) Today we're looking at ClawGym II: Exploring Black-Box RL on Agent Harness, by Huatong Song, Fei Bai, and Ming Yang, with seventeen more colleagues spread across the Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence at Renmin University of China and a lab called IQuest Research. Here's the uncomfortable premise. The agents everyone actually deploys are not naked language models. They're models wrapped in a harness: a planning loop, tool invocations, memory reads and writes, retry logic, maybe a sub-agent or two. And yet almost all reinforcement learning for agents is done on the naked model, on synthetic traces, with the harness treated as something that happens later, at deployment, to someone else. This paper declines that arrangement. It trains the full stack, model plus harness, as one unit, using reinforcement learning that never opens either of them up. The harness stays a black box. The model stays a black box. All the learning signal comes from the outside: did the finished trajectory complete the task, yes or no. That refusal raises the obvious question, which is also why the paper exists: how do you make reinforcement learning work at all when your policy is a sprawling scaffold that takes hundreds of steps per episode? Three reasons, and the paper is upfront about all of them. First, episodes are enormous. A single rollout through a real harness on a real task can run for hundreds of turns, and because the whole running conversation ships back to the model on every one of them, total token spend grows much faster than the episode does. item.title: How Do Agents Fail on AutoResearch: End-to-End Diagnostic Evaluation on 100 Real-World Frontier Research Tasks
item.description: By Yanlin Fei, Nazhou Liu, Xinmiao Yu, et al. (Prentis AI, Stanford University, Titan Holdings) Welcome back to the show. What actually breaks when you hand a hundred real research problems to a frontier coding agent and let it run unsupervised? We finally have a careful answer, and it isn't flattered. The paper is "How Do Agents Fail on AutoResearch: End-to-End Diagnostic Evaluation on 100 Real-World Frontier Research Tasks," by Yanlin Fei, Nazhou Liu, and Xinmiao Yu, with colleagues at Prentis AI, Stanford University, and Titan Holdings. Found it, documented it, shipped it. That yielded 800 full trajectories, roughly seventy-three thousand tool calls, averaging ninety-two steps per run. Scoring those runs is the second contribution.
